texts.title: Bread After the Night Shift
texts.summary: A hospital cleaner and an old baker share a roll every morning, until the bakery suddenly closes.

parts: Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] started at ten at night. It ended at six in the morning.
After work, she always stopped at a small bakery. It was her [habit]. The baker was an old man. His name was Mr. Haddad.
Every morning, there was a warm roll for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he said. He never let her pay.
At first, they were [strangers|stranger]. Then they started to talk. He told her about his fig tree. She told him about her son in college.
One Monday, the bakery was dark. The door was locked. On Tuesday and Wednesday, it was still closed.
Rosa was [worried]. She asked the woman at the flower shop next door. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” the woman said. “His heart.”
It was Rosa’s hospital! That night, she went to work early. She found his room. He looked small and tired in the bed.
She put a roll on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad laughed.
Rosa visited him every night before her shift. Slowly, he began to [recover]. Three weeks later, the bakery opened again.
In the window there was a new sign. It said, “Fresh bread every morning. Thank you, Rosa.”
Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] started at ten at night and ended at six in the morning. When she walked home, the streets were gray and quiet.
On her way, she always stopped at a small bakery on Elm Street. It was her [habit]. The baker, Mr. Haddad, was an old man with flour on his glasses.
Every morning, a warm roll was waiting for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he said, and he never let her pay.
At first, they were [strangers|stranger]. But slowly, they started to talk. He told her about the fig tree in his yard. She told him about her son, who was in college far away.
Then one Monday, the bakery was dark. The door was locked. On Tuesday and Wednesday, it was still closed.
Rosa felt [worried]. She asked the woman at the flower shop next door. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” the woman said. “It’s his heart.”
It was the city hospital. It was her hospital. That night, Rosa came to work early and found his room on the fourth floor. He looked small and tired in the big bed.
She put a roll from the cafeteria on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad laughed for the first time in days.
After that, Rosa visited him every night before her shift. Slowly, he began to [recover]. Three weeks later, the bakery opened again.
In the window there was a new sign. It said, “Fresh bread every morning. Thank you, Rosa.”

Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] began at ten at night and ended at six in the morning, when the sky was turning from black to gray and the first buses were starting their routes. By then her arms were heavy and her feet hurt, but she liked the walk home through the quiet streets.

Halfway home, on the corner of Elm Street, there was a small bakery with a green door. Stopping there had become a [habit] she didn’t even think about anymore. The baker, Mr. Haddad, was a small old man who always had flour on his glasses and a radio playing old songs in the back.
Every morning, a warm roll wrapped in paper was waiting for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he would say. When she tried to pay, he waved her money away as if it were a fly.

At first, they were [strangers|stranger] who shared a few polite words. But mornings add up. Over the months, he told her about the fig tree in his yard that gave far too many figs, and about the city where he was born. She told him about her son, who was studying engineering at a college eight hours away and called her every Sunday.

Then, one Monday, the green door was locked and the windows were dark. Rosa stood there for a minute, holding her bag, feeling strange without the warm paper in her hand. On Tuesday the bakery was still closed. On Wednesday too.

Rosa grew more and more [worried]. On Wednesday, she stepped into the flower shop next door. The owner looked at her sadly. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” she said. “It’s his heart. He has no family here.”
“Which hospital?” Rosa asked, but she already knew. There was only one in this part of the city. It was her hospital.

That night, she came to work an hour early and asked at the front desk. She found him on the fourth floor, in a room at the end of a long hallway. He looked smaller than she remembered, lost in the white sheets, with a tube in his arm and nothing on his table.

Rosa took a roll out of her bag. It was from the hospital cafeteria, dry and a little sad. She set it on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad stared at her, and then he laughed so hard that a nurse looked in to check on him.

After that, Rosa visited him every night before her shift. She brought him the newspaper and told him what was happening on Elm Street. Slowly, he began to [recover]. Three weeks later, the green door was open again, and the smell of bread reached the corner before she did.
In the window, next to the price list, was a new sign written in careful letters: “Fresh bread every morning. Thank you, Rosa.” And on the counter, as always, a warm roll was waiting.

texts.title: Grandma’s Bread on the Screen
texts.summary: A woman far from home learns her grandmother’s bread over video calls.

parts: Leyla lived in a new country. She had a good job and nice friends. But on Sunday mornings, she was [homesick]. She missed her grandmother’s bread.
One Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. “Teach me your bread,” she said. Her grandmother laughed.
“Flour, water, salt and a little oil,” her grandmother said. “Those are the [ingredients|ingredient].”
“How much flour?” Leyla asked. “One cup? Two cups?” Her grandmother never [measured|measure] anything. She held up her hand. “A [handful]. Then another.”
Leyla mixed everything. Then she [kneaded|knead] the [dough]. She pushed it again and again. Her arms hurt. “Harder!” said her grandmother on the screen.
The first bread was flat and hard. Leyla almost cried.
“My first bread was worse,” her grandmother said. “Try again next Sunday.”
Leyla tried every Sunday. On the fifth Sunday, the bread was round, soft and warm. It smelled like her grandmother’s house.
Leyla held the bread up to the camera. Her grandmother clapped. Home did not feel so far away.
Leyla had lived in the new country for two years. She had a good job and kind friends, but on cold Sunday mornings she was still [homesick]. Most of all, she missed her grandmother’s bread.
So one Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. It was morning for Leyla and evening in the village. “Teach me how to make your bread,” Leyla said. Her grandmother laughed and put on her glasses.
“Flour, water, salt and a little oil,” her grandmother said. “Those are the only [ingredients|ingredient]. The rest is in your hands.”
Leyla had a measuring cup ready. “How much flour? One cup? Two?” Her grandmother never [measured|measure] anything. She held up her hand. “A [handful]. Then another. Then you feel it.”
Leyla leaned the phone against the sugar jar and started to mix.

Next, she had to [knead] the [dough]. She pushed it, folded it and pushed it again. After five minutes, her arms hurt. “Harder!” her grandmother said from the screen. “Use your shoulders, not just your fingers!”
An hour later, Leyla took the bread out of the oven. It was flat and hard, like a stone. She almost cried.
“My first bread was worse,” her grandmother said. “My mother gave it to the chickens. Try again next Sunday.”
Every Sunday for a month, Leyla called, and every Sunday the bread got a little better.
On the fifth Sunday, she pulled a round, golden loaf from the oven. She broke it open, and the warm smell filled her small kitchen. It smelled exactly like her grandmother’s house.
Leyla held the bread up to the camera. On the other side of the world, her grandmother clapped her hands. For the first time in a long time, home did not feel so far away.

Leyla had lived in the new country for two years. She had a steady job at a pharmacy, a small apartment with good light, and friends who invited her to dinner. Still, on gray Sunday mornings, she felt [homesick] in a way that was hard to explain. What she missed most was not a place but a smell: her grandmother’s bread, coming out of the oven while the whole house was still waking up.

So one Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. It was nine in the morning for Leyla and late afternoon in the village. Her grandmother’s face filled the screen, a little too close, the way it always did. “Teach me your bread,” Leyla said. Her grandmother laughed, went to find her glasses, and came back looking very serious.
“Flour, water, salt, a little oil,” she said, counting on her fingers. “Those are all the [ingredients|ingredient]. The rest is in your hands.”

Leyla had a measuring cup and a kitchen scale ready on the counter. “How much flour, exactly? One cup? Two?” But her grandmother had never [measured|measure] anything in her life. She held up one wrinkled hand. “A [handful]. Then another. Then you stop thinking and you feel it.”
Leyla leaned the phone against the sugar jar, rolled up her sleeves and began to mix.

Then came the hard part. She had to [knead] the [dough], pushing it away with the heels of her hands, folding it back, turning it, pushing again. After five minutes, her arms ached. “Harder!” her grandmother called from the screen. “Use your shoulders, not just your fingers! You’re petting it, not making bread!”
An hour later, Leyla opened the oven. The loaf was flat, pale and hard enough to knock on. She stared at it, and to her surprise, her eyes filled with tears.
Her grandmother only shrugged. “My first bread was worse,” she said. “My mother gave it to the chickens, and even the chickens complained. Call me next Sunday.”
So Leyla called the next Sunday, and the one after that. Each week, the bread was a little softer and a little rounder. Each week, they talked a little longer after it came out of the oven.

On the fifth Sunday, Leyla pulled out a round, golden loaf that sounded hollow when she tapped the bottom, just as her grandmother had taught her. She tore it open, and steam rose into the cold kitchen. The smell was exactly right.

She held the bread up to the camera. Thousands of miles away, her grandmother clapped her hands and called the neighbors to come and look. Leyla laughed, a piece of warm bread in her hand, and for the first time in a long time, home did not feel so far away.

texts.title: Your Car Repair Estimate
texts.summary: A mechanic texts what is wrong with a car, what the repair costs, and how to say yes.

parts: Hillside Auto: Hi Luis! This is Tom. I am the [mechanic] working on your car.
We checked your car today. The noise comes from your front [brakes|brake]. The brake pads are very thin. We need to change them soon. Then your car is safe.
Your tires are fine. They don’t need any work.
Here is our [estimate] for the brakes:
Parts: $140
[Labor|labor]: $120 (about 2 hours)
Total: $260, plus tax
There is a 12-month [warranty] on the parts and the labor.
Do you want us to do the work? Reply YES. Please [approve] it by 2:00 p.m. today. Then your car is ready tomorrow, Wednesday, by 4:00 p.m.
You don’t want the work? Reply NO. Then you only pay $40 for the check. You can pick up your car before 6:00 p.m.
Questions? Call us at 555-0187.

texts.title: Let’s Talk About Your Child
texts.summary: A teacher invites a family to a short meeting about their child’s year.

parts: Dear Mateo’s family,
I want to meet with you. We can talk about Mateo at school. This meeting is called a parent-teacher [conference].
We will talk about Mateo’s [progress] in reading and math. You can ask me questions too.
Each conference is about 20 minutes.
I am [available] at these times:
Tuesday, November 17, from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m.
Wednesday, November 18, from 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. School ends early that day, at 12:30.
Please [sign up] for a time. Fill out the form at the bottom of this note. Put it in Mateo’s folder by Monday, November 9.
Do you need an [interpreter]? We can have one there. It is free. Write your language on the form.
Thank you, Ms. Patel, Room 12
Dear Mateo’s family,
I would like to invite you to a parent-teacher [conference] to talk about Mateo’s year so far.
We will look at his [progress] in reading and math, and you can ask me any questions. Each conference will take about 20 minutes.
I am [available] at these times:
Tuesday, November 17, from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m.
Wednesday, November 18, from 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. On this day, school ends early, at 12:30.
To [sign up], fill out the form at the bottom of this note and put it in Mateo’s folder by Monday, November 9.
If you would like an [interpreter], write your language on the form, and we will have one there for free.
If none of these times work for you, write a note on the form. We can find another time or talk on the phone.
Thank you, Ms. Patel, Room 12
Dear Mateo’s family,
It has been a wonderful start to the year in Room 12. I would like to invite you to a parent-teacher [conference] so we can talk about how Mateo is doing.

During our meeting, we will look at samples of his work and talk about his [progress] in reading and math. I will share what he does well and what we are working on next. This is also a good time for you to ask questions or tell me anything that might help Mateo at school. Each conference will last about 20 minutes.
I am [available] at the following times:
Tuesday, November 17, from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m.
Wednesday, November 18, from 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. Please remember that students will be dismissed early, at 12:30, on this day.

To [sign up], please fill out the form at the bottom of this note, choose two times that work for you, and return it in Mateo’s folder by Monday, November 9. I will send a note back to confirm your time.
If you would like an [interpreter], please write your language on the form. We will have one at the meeting at no cost to you.
If none of these times work for your family, just write a note on the form. We can find another time or have the conference by phone.
I look forward to meeting you and working together this year.
Warmly, Ms. Rachel Patel, Third grade, Room 12, Cedar Hill Elementary School

texts.title: Your New Debit Card Is Here
texts.summary: A bank sends a new debit card and explains how to start using it safely.

parts: Dear Ms. Hassan,
Here is your new [debit card]. It is in this envelope.
Your old card [expires|expire] at the end of November. It stops working on Monday, November 30.
Your bank [account] does not change. Your money is safe.
First, [activate] your new card. Call us at 1-800-555-0142. Or use the Lakeview app.
Then you choose a [PIN|pin]. A PIN is a secret number. It has four numbers. You need it at a store or an ATM.
Is your new card working? Then cut your old card into small pieces.
Never tell anyone your PIN. We never call, text or email to ask for it. Someone asks for it? That is [fraud]. Call us right away.
Customer Service, Lakeview Community Bank
Dear Ms. Hassan,
Your new Lakeview Community Bank [debit card] is in this envelope. Your old card, ending in 4821, [expires|expire] at the end of November. It will stop working on Monday, November 30.

Before you can use your new card, you must [activate] it. To do this, call our automated line at 1-800-555-0142, or sign in to the Lakeview app and choose “Activate card.” It takes about two minutes.

During activation, you will choose a four-digit [PIN|pin]. You will need this PIN for purchases at stores and for cash at ATMs. Choose a number that is easy for you to remember but hard for others to guess, and do not use your birthday.
Once your new card is working, please cut your old card into small pieces and throw it away.

Protect your PIN. Lakeview Community Bank will never call, text or email you to ask for your PIN or your full card number. If someone contacts you and asks for this information, it is [fraud]. Do not share anything. Hang up and call us at 1-800-555-0142, which is open 24 hours a day.
If your card is ever lost or stolen, call the same number right away so we can lock it.
Thank you for banking with us.
Sincerely, Customer Service, Lakeview Community Bank

texts.title: Learning to Drive at Forty
texts.summary: A mother who has never driven decides to get her license at forty.

parts: Amara was forty years old. She did not have a driver’s [license]. Every day, she took two buses to work. The trip took ninety minutes.
One night, she said, “I want to learn to drive.” Her daughter, Joy, was surprised. “Mom, you are forty!” “Yes,” said Amara. “And I am tired of buses.”
Her [instructor] was Mr. Lee. He was calm and kind. In the first lesson, Amara pushed the [brake] too hard. The car stopped very fast. “Gently,” said Mr. Lee. “Keep your hands [steady].”
Amara practiced every Saturday for three months. She learned to look in the [mirror] and to park.
Then she took the driving test. She was very nervous. She did not stop at a stop sign. She failed the test.
That night, Amara was sad. “I am too old,” she said. But Joy said, “You always tell me not to quit. So don’t quit.”
One month later, Amara took the test again. She drove slowly and carefully. She passed!
The next Monday, Amara drove to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She felt proud and [confident].
Amara was forty years old, and she had never driven a car. Every morning, she took two buses to her job at the hospital. The trip took ninety minutes each way, in rain, snow and summer heat.

One night at dinner, she made an announcement. “I’m going to get my driver’s [license].” Her daughter, Joy, who was seventeen, almost dropped her fork. “Mom, you’re forty!” “Yes,” Amara said. “And I’m tired of waiting for buses.”

Her driving [instructor], Mr. Lee, was a calm man with a soft voice. In the first lesson, Amara pressed the [brake] so hard that they both flew forward against their seat belts. “Gently,” Mr. Lee said, as if nothing had happened. “Keep your hands [steady]. The car will listen to you.”
Every Saturday for three months, she practiced. She learned to check her [mirror] before changing lanes, to park between two cars, and to stay calm when other drivers honked.
Then it was time for the test. Her hands were wet on the wheel. At the second corner, she forgot to stop completely at a stop sign. The test was over in ten minutes. She did not pass.
That night, Amara sat in the kitchen and said she was too old for this. Joy put her phone down. “You always tell me not to quit,” she said. “So don’t quit.”

A month later, Amara took the test again. This time, she drove slowly and carefully, and she stopped at every stop sign for a full three seconds. When it was over, the examiner smiled and said, “Congratulations.”

The next Monday, Amara drove herself to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She parked, turned off the engine and sat for a moment, feeling proud and [confident]. Then she called Joy. “I’m here,” she said. “And I’m early.”

Amara was forty years old, and she had never driven a car. In the town where she grew up, almost no one owned one, and in her first years in this country there had been no money and no time. So every morning, she took two buses to her job at the hospital: ninety minutes there and ninety minutes back, in freezing rain, in snow, in summer heat that made the bus windows sweat.

One night at dinner, she set down her spoon and made an announcement. “I’m going to get my driver’s [license].” Her daughter, Joy, who was seventeen, nearly choked on her rice. “Mom. You’re forty.” “I know how old I am,” Amara said. “I’m also tired of standing at bus stops.”

Her driving [instructor], Mr. Lee, was a calm, gray-haired man who spoke as softly as a librarian. In their first lesson, Amara stepped on the [brake] so hard that they both flew forward against their seat belts. Mr. Lee simply straightened his glasses. “Gently,” he said. “Keep your hands [steady]. The car will do what you ask. You only have to ask nicely.”

Every Saturday for three months, she practiced. She learned to check her [mirror] before every lane change, to squeeze into a parking space between two cars, and to keep breathing when a truck honked behind her. Some lessons went well. After others, she sat in the parking lot and wondered what she was doing.

Then came the test. Her palms were wet on the wheel before she even started the engine. At the second corner, trying to think about everything at once, she rolled through a stop sign without stopping completely. The examiner made a mark on his clipboard, and the test was over in ten minutes. She had failed.

That night, Amara sat at the kitchen table and announced that she was too old for this, that some people were simply not made for driving. Joy put down her phone, which was rare. “You always tell me not to quit when things get hard,” she said. “So don’t quit.” Amara had no answer for that, which was also rare.

A month later, she took the test again. This time she drove slowly and carefully, as if she were carrying a full cup of tea. She stopped at every stop sign and counted to three. When they pulled back into the lot, the examiner, the same man as before, looked up from his clipboard and smiled. “Congratulations,” he said.

The next Monday, Amara drove herself to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She pulled into the hospital parking lot, turned off the engine and sat for a moment in the quiet, feeling something she had not expected: not just proud, but [confident], as if a door she had thought was locked had been open the whole time. Then she called Joy. “I’m here,” she said. “And for once, I’m early.”

texts.title: Why Your Electric Bill Is Higher
texts.summary: An electric company explains a high bill and offers a way to pay it in parts.

parts: Dear Mr. Haddad,
Your electric bill for September is $237. Most months, your bill is about $110. Why is this bill higher?
We read your [meter] on October 5. Your electricity [usage] was very high. You used about two times the electricity of a normal month.
September was very hot. Many people used their air conditioners a lot. We checked the meter. It is correct.
This bill is [due] on Friday, November 13. Is it hard to pay it all at once? You can use a [payment plan].
With the plan, you pay in three [installments|installment]. Each installment is $79. It goes on your bill in November, December, and January. The plan is free.
Do you want the plan? Call us at 1-800-555-0142. Or sign in to your account on our website. Do this before November 13.
No payment and no plan by November 13? Then you pay a [late fee] of $15.
Customer Service, Riverbend Electric

Your electric bill for September is $237. Your bill is usually about $110, so we want to explain why this bill is higher.

We checked the meter reading, and it is correct.

To join the plan, call us at 1-800-555-0142 or sign in to your account on our website before November 13.
If you do not pay the bill or join the plan by November 13, we will add a [late fee] of $15.

parts: Free English Classes for Adults!
Come to the Oak Street Community Center, 215 Oak Street.
Classes start on Tuesday, November 10. They are on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. The last class is on Thursday, December 17. There is no class on Thanksgiving, Thursday, November 26.
We have three levels: [beginner], middle and [advanced]. Books are free too.
First, take a short [placement test]. It shows your level. The test is on Saturday, November 7, from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. It takes about 30 minutes.
Do you have children? We have free [childcare] during class. It is for children 3 to 10 years old.
Please [register] by Thursday, November 5. Go to oakstreetcenter.org/english. Or call Joy Mendez at 555-0188.
All adults are welcome!
Free English Classes for Adults!
The Oak Street Community Center has free English classes for adults. The center is at 215 Oak Street, and the number 6 bus stops in front.
Classes start on Tuesday, November 10, and end on Thursday, December 17. Classes meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. There is no class on Thanksgiving, Thursday, November 26.
We have three levels: [beginner], intermediate and [advanced]. If you are new to English, the beginner class is for you. Books are free.

Before classes start, please take a short [placement test] on Saturday, November 7, between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. The placement test helps us find the right level for you. It takes about 30 minutes.
Do you have young children? We have free [childcare] during class for children ages 3 to 10.
To join, please [register] by Thursday, November 5. You can register online at oakstreetcenter.org/english, or call Joy Mendez at 555-0188.
All adults are welcome. Bring a notebook and a pen!
Free English Classes for Adults!

Do you want to speak English with more confidence at work, at the doctor’s office or at your child’s school? The Oak Street Community Center offers free English classes for adults of all backgrounds. The center is located at 215 Oak Street, and the number 6 bus stops right out front.

The fall session begins on Tuesday, November 10, and ends on Thursday, December 17. Classes meet every Tuesday and Thursday from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. There will be no class on Thanksgiving, Thursday, November 26.

We offer three levels: [beginner], intermediate and [advanced]. The beginner class is a great place to start if you know only a few words. The advanced class focuses on writing, reading longer texts and job interviews. All books and materials are free.

Every new student takes a short [placement test] on Saturday, November 7, any time between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. The placement test helps us find the right level for you, and it takes about 30 minutes. It is not graded, so there is nothing to study.
Parents, don’t let childcare stop you! We provide free [childcare] during class for children ages 3 to 10, in a safe room just down the hall.
Space is limited, so please [register] by Thursday, November 5. You can register online at oakstreetcenter.org/english, call Joy Mendez at 555-0188, or stop by the front desk.
All adults are welcome. Just bring a notebook, a pen and a smile!

header.subject: Field trip to the science museum

parts: Dear families,
Our class will go on a [field trip]. We will go to the Greenway Science Museum. The trip is on Thursday, November 12.
The children will see a show about the stars. They will see animals too.
The bus leaves the school at 9:00 a.m. It comes back at 2:30 p.m.
Your child needs a [permission slip]. It is in the red folder. Please sign it.
The [fee] is $8. It pays for the bus and the tickets.
The slip and the money are [due] on Friday, November 6. Is $8 a problem for you? Call the school office. Every child can go.
Please pack a lunch and a water bottle for your child.
Can you come with us? We need four [chaperones|chaperone]. A chaperone helps a small group of children. Please email me by November 6.
Thank you! Ms. Ortiz
Dear families,

Every child needs a signed [permission slip] to go. The slip is in your child’s red folder.

Thank you!

texts.title: The First Night in the Kitchen
texts.summary: On his first night at a busy restaurant, a new kitchen worker makes a big mistake.

parts: Tomás had a new job in a restaurant kitchen. It was his first night. His [shift] started at four o’clock.
The head cook, Rosa, gave him a white [apron]. “Wash the dishes and cut the onions,” she said. “Don’t try to be fast. Fast comes later.”
The kitchen was hot and loud. Everyone moved very fast.
At seven o’clock, the restaurant was full. Rosa asked Tomás to carry a big pot of soup.
He walked too fast. He did not see the wet floor. He fell, and the soup [spilled|spill] everywhere.
Everyone stopped. Tomás felt [embarrassed]. His face was red. He did not want to look at anyone.
Rosa helped him stand up. “Are you hurt?” she asked. “No,” he said. “I am sorry.”
Rosa smiled. “On my first day, I dropped a box of eggs,” she said. “Now I run this kitchen.”
Her words [encouraged|encourage] him. He cleaned the floor and went back to work.
At midnight, Rosa said, “See you tomorrow.” Tomás went home tired, but he felt more [confident].
Tomás started his new job at Casa Verde on a Friday, the busiest night of the week. His [shift] began at four o’clock, and he arrived twenty minutes early.
The head cook, Rosa, handed him a white [apron]. “Wash the dishes, cut the onions, and watch how we work,” she said. “Don’t worry about being fast. Fast comes later.”
By seven o’clock, every table was full. The kitchen was hot and loud, and people called out orders over the noise. Tomás cut so many onions that his eyes would not stop watering.
Then Rosa asked him to bring a big pot of soup to the front. He walked quickly to show that he could keep up. He didn’t see the wet spot on the floor.
His feet slid, and the pot hit the ground. Hot soup [spilled|spill] across the floor.
The whole kitchen went quiet. Tomás felt so [embarrassed] that he couldn’t look at anyone. He was sure he would lose the job on his very first night.
Rosa walked over and helped him up. “Are you hurt?” she asked. He shook his head and said he was sorry.
“On my first day here, I dropped a whole box of eggs,” she told him. “Twenty-four eggs. Now I run this kitchen.”

Her story [encouraged|encourage] him. He cleaned the floor, washed his hands and went back to the onions. At midnight, Rosa said, “See you tomorrow.” Tomás walked home tired, but more [confident] than when he came.

Tomás started his new job at Casa Verde on a Friday, which everyone later told him was a terrible choice. Friday was the busiest night of the week. His [shift] began at four o’clock, but he arrived twenty minutes early and stood outside the back door, reading the same text message from the manager three times.

Inside, the head cook, a small woman named Rosa with flour on her sleeves, handed him a white [apron]. “Dishes first, then onions,” she said. “And watch how we move. Don’t try to be fast tonight. Fast comes later.”

By seven, every table in the dining room was full. The kitchen was hot, the fans roared, and orders flew over the noise in two languages. Tomás cut onions until his eyes streamed and his fingers smelled like them.

Then Rosa called his name. “Soup for table six. Bring the big pot to the front.” Tomás wanted to show that he could keep up, so he walked faster than he should have. He never saw the puddle near the sink.
His feet slid out from under him. The pot hit the tiles with a crash, and hot soup [spilled|spill] in a wide orange wave across the floor.

For a moment, the whole kitchen went silent. Even the fans seemed quieter. Tomás felt so [embarrassed] that he could not lift his eyes from the mess. He was certain that his first night would also be his last.
Rosa reached him first and helped him to his feet. “Are you burned?” she asked. He shook his head and started to apologize, but she held up a hand.
“My first day here, eleven years ago, I dropped a whole box of eggs,” she said. “Twenty-four eggs, all over the owner’s shoes. Now I run this kitchen.”

Somebody laughed, then somebody else, and the noise came back. Rosa’s story [encouraged|encourage] him more than any kind speech could have. He mopped the floor, washed his hands and went back to his onions. At midnight, as he hung up his apron, Rosa said simply, “See you tomorrow.” Tomás walked home with sore feet, feeling more [confident] than he had in months.

texts.title: Hoa’s First Interview
texts.summary: A woman from Vietnam goes to her first job interview in the United States and forgets everything she practiced.

parts: Hoa came to the United States from Vietnam eight months ago. In Vietnam, she took care of the money for her family’s shop. She did this for ten years.
Today she had her first job [interview] in America. It was at a store called Parkside Furniture. The job was office assistant.
Hoa was very [nervous]. Every night that week, she practiced with her son, Minh. He asked questions, and she answered.
At the store, the manager, Mr. Kessler, shook her hand. He asked, “What is your biggest [strength]?” Hoa forgot her answer. She could not say a word.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “My [accent] is strong.” Mr. Kessler smiled. “My mother has an accent too,” he said. “I understand you fine. Take your time.”
Hoa felt better. She told the truth. “I took care of the money for my family’s shop for ten years. I am careful with numbers. I never made a big mistake.”
“That is the [experience] we need,” Mr. Kessler said.
Two days later, her phone rang. Parkside Furniture [hired|hire] her. That night, Minh made dinner for his mother.
Hoa moved to the United States from Vietnam eight months ago. Back home, she took care of all the money for her family’s shop for ten years. Here, she was starting again.
Today she had her first job [interview] in America, at a store called Parkside Furniture. The job was office assistant: answering the phone, typing, and keeping records.
Hoa was very [nervous]. Every night that week, she practiced at the kitchen table with her son, Minh. He asked questions, and she answered them in English, again and again.
At the store, the manager, Mr. Kessler, shook her hand and gave her a glass of water. Then he asked, “What would you say is your biggest [strength]?”
Hoa opened her mouth, but nothing came out. She had practiced this question ten times, and now she couldn’t remember a single word.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “My [accent] is strong.” Mr. Kessler smiled. “My mother has an accent too,” he said. “I understand you just fine. Take your time.”

Hoa took a breath. She stopped trying to remember her answer and just told the truth. “For ten years, I took care of the money for my family’s shop,” she said. “I am careful with numbers. In ten years, I never made a big mistake.”
Mr. Kessler wrote something down. “That’s exactly the kind of [experience] we need,” he said.
Two days later, her phone rang. Parkside Furniture had [hired|hire] her. That night, Minh cooked dinner for his mother, and they ate it on the good plates.

Hoa had moved to the United States from Vietnam eight months earlier. Back home, she had taken care of all the money for her family’s small hardware shop for ten years: the bills, the taxes, the long columns of numbers in a green notebook. Here, nobody knew any of that. Here, she was starting again.

This morning she had her first job [interview] in America, at a store called Parkside Furniture. The job was office assistant, which meant answering the phone, typing, and keeping records of orders and payments. She had read the job post so many times she could say it with her eyes closed.

She was terribly [nervous]. Every night that week, after dinner, she had practiced at the kitchen table with her son, Minh. He played the manager, frowning and asking questions in a deep voice, and she answered in English, again and again, until they were both laughing.

At the store, the manager, Mr. Kessler, shook her hand, brought her a glass of water, and sat down across from her in a small office that smelled like new wood. He looked at her résumé for a moment. Then he asked, “So, what would you say is your biggest [strength]?”

Hoa opened her mouth, and nothing came out. She had practiced this exact question ten times. Minh had even written her answer on a card. Now, in this quiet room, she couldn’t remember a single word of it.

“I’m sorry,” she said finally, looking at the table. “My [accent] is strong.” Mr. Kessler smiled. “My mother has an accent too,” he said. “She came here from Poland. I understand you just fine. Take your time.”

Hoa took a long breath. She stopped trying to find the words on Minh’s card and simply told the truth. “For ten years, I took care of the money for my family’s shop,” she said. “I am very careful with numbers. In ten years, I never made a big mistake. Not one.”
Mr. Kessler wrote something down and underlined it. “That’s exactly the kind of [experience] we need,” he said.

Two days later, while she was folding laundry, her phone rang. Parkside Furniture had [hired|hire] her, and she could start on Monday. That night, Minh cooked dinner for his mother for the first time, and they ate it on the good plates.

texts.title: How Does a Rainbow Form?
texts.summary: Sunlight is a mix of colors. Tiny raindrops bend the light and spread the colors apart, and we see a rainbow.

parts: After the rain, the sun comes out. Sometimes you see a rainbow in the sky. How does it happen?
Sunlight looks white. But it is really a [mix] of many colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet.
After rain, the air is full of tiny water [droplets|droplet]. Sunlight goes into each droplet. The light [bends|bend]. Each color bends a little differently, so the colors move apart.
Inside the droplet, the light hits the back and [reflects|reflect], like in a mirror. Then it comes out again. Now we can see each color.
A rainbow is a big [arc]. Red is on the outside. Violet is on the inside.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you. The rain must be in front of you.
Sometimes you see two rainbows. The second one is [fainter|faint]. Its colors are in the opposite order.
You may see a rainbow when the sun comes out after rain, near a waterfall, or even in the spray of a garden hose. It looks almost like magic, but there is a simple reason for it.

Sunlight looks white, but it is really a [mix] of colors. You can see these colors in a rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. Long ago, the scientist Isaac Newton used a piece of glass called a prism to show that white light can be split into these colors.
After rain, the air is full of tiny water [droplets|droplet]. When sunlight goes into a droplet, it [bends|bend] a little. Each color bends by a different amount, so the colors begin to spread apart.

The light then hits the back of the droplet and [reflects|reflect], almost like light in a mirror. As it comes out of the droplet, it bends again, and the colors spread out even more. Millions of droplets do this at the same time, and together they make a rainbow.

A rainbow is shaped like a big [arc], with red on the outside and violet on the inside. To see one, you must stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. That is why rainbows are most common in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low in the sky.
Sometimes there is a second rainbow above the first. It is [fainter|faint], and its colors are in the opposite order. From an airplane, people can sometimes see a rainbow as a full circle.

A rainbow can appear when the sun breaks through after a storm, in the mist of a waterfall, or in the spray of a garden hose on a summer day. People have told stories about rainbows for thousands of years, but the science behind them is surprisingly simple.

Sunlight seems white, but it is actually a [mix] of all the colors we can see. In the 1660s, Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and watched it spread into a band of colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. He also showed that a second prism could bring the colors back together into white light.

Raindrops act like millions of tiny prisms. When a ray of sunlight enters a water [droplet], it slows down and [bends|bend]. Each color bends by a slightly different amount, violet the most and red the least, so the colors begin to separate.

The light then travels to the back of the droplet, where it [reflects|reflect] and heads back toward the front. As it leaves the droplet, it bends once more, spreading the colors even further apart. From where you stand, each droplet sends only one color toward your eye, so the rainbow you see is built from the light of millions of different drops.

Because of the angles involved, a rainbow always forms a curved [arc] around the point directly opposite the sun, with red on the outside edge and violet on the inside. You can only see one with the sun at your back and rain in front of you, and the sun must be fairly low, which is why rainbows are most often seen in the morning or late afternoon.

Sometimes a second, [fainter|faint] rainbow appears above the first. It forms when light reflects twice inside each droplet, and this reverses the order of its colors. Seen from an airplane, a rainbow can even form a complete circle. And because a rainbow depends on exactly where you stand, no two people ever see quite the same one.

texts.title: How Do Bees Make Honey?
texts.summary: Honey starts as a sweet liquid inside flowers. Thousands of bees work together to change it.

parts: Honey comes from bees. But bees do not find honey. They make it.
Bees live together in a [hive]. A big group of bees is called a [colony].
Bees fly to flowers. Many flowers have a sweet liquid inside. It is called [nectar]. A bee drinks the nectar. It keeps the nectar in a special stomach.
The bee flies back to the hive. It gives the nectar to other bees. They pass it from bee to bee. The nectar slowly changes.
Next, the bees put it in very small rooms made of [wax]. They move their wings fast, like fans. This dries the nectar. Now it is thick honey.
Then the bees [seal] each room with wax. The honey is food for the winter.
Bees also carry [pollen] from flower to flower. This helps plants make fruit and seeds.
Honey is one of the oldest sweet foods people eat. But where does it come from? Bees make it, and it takes a lot of teamwork.
Honeybees live together in a [hive]. One hive is home to a [colony] of thousands of bees. Each bee has a job.

Some bees fly out to find flowers. Inside many flowers is a sweet liquid called [nectar]. A bee drinks the nectar with its long tongue and keeps it in a special “honey stomach.” A bee may visit hundreds of flowers on one trip.
Back at the hive, the bee passes the nectar to younger bees. They pass it from mouth to mouth. Each time, the bees add natural chemicals that slowly change the nectar.

Next, the bees put the nectar into tiny six-sided rooms made of [wax]. Fresh nectar has a lot of water in it, so the bees beat their wings to move air over it. Slowly, the water dries up, and the nectar becomes thick, sticky honey.
When the honey is ready, the bees [seal] each room with a thin cap of wax. The colony will eat this honey in winter, when there are no flowers.
One bee makes only a tiny amount of honey in her whole life, much less than a spoonful. That is why a jar of honey needs the work of many thousands of bees.

Bees also help us in another way. As they move from flower to flower, they carry [pollen]. This helps plants make fruit and seeds. Many of the fruits and vegetables we eat need bees and other insects to grow.

People have been eating honey for thousands of years; ancient rock paintings even show people collecting it from wild bees. Yet few of us stop to think about how it is made. The answer is a remarkable example of teamwork.
Honeybees live in a [hive], where a single [colony] can contain tens of thousands of bees. Almost all of them are female worker bees, and each one has a job that changes as she gets older.

The older workers are the foragers. They fly out, sometimes several kilometers from home, in search of flowers. Deep inside many blossoms is a sugary liquid called [nectar]. A forager sucks it up through her long, tube-like tongue and stores it in a special honey stomach, separate from the stomach she uses for her own food. She may visit hundreds of flowers before she heads home.
At the hive, she passes the nectar to younger house bees, who pass it from one to another. Along the way, they add enzymes, natural chemicals that break the sugars in the nectar into simpler ones.

The bees then place the nectar into the honeycomb, a pattern of six-sided cells made of [wax] that the bees produce from their own bodies. Fresh nectar is mostly water, so the bees fan it with their wings, creating a steady flow of warm air. Over several days, much of the water dries up, and the nectar thickens into honey.
Once it is ready, the bees [seal] each cell with a thin wax cap. Stored this way, honey keeps for a very long time. It is the colony’s food supply for the winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
For all this effort, one worker bee produces only a tiny amount in her lifetime, a small fraction of a teaspoon. A single jar of honey is the life’s work of many thousands of bees.

Bees give us something even more valuable than honey, though. As they travel from blossom to blossom, grains of [pollen] stick to their hairy bodies and rub off on the next flower. This process, called pollination, helps many plants produce fruit and seeds, including many of the crops people depend on.

texts.title: How Do Birds Find Their Way?
texts.summary: Every year, many birds fly very long distances. They use the sun, the stars, and even the Earth itself to find the way.

parts: In the fall, many birds fly away to warm places. In the spring, they come back. We say these birds [migrate].
Why do they go? In winter, it is cold. It is hard to find food. So the birds fly to places with more food. In spring, they come back to make nests and have babies.
The [journey] can be very long. One bird, the Arctic tern, flies from the far north to the far south and back every year. How do birds know the way?
In the day, many birds use the sun. At night, many birds use the stars.
The Earth has a [magnetic field]. People cannot feel it. But birds can. It helps them know where north is, even on a cloudy day.
Birds also look for [landmarks|landmark]. These are things that are easy to see, like rivers, mountains, and the coast. Many birds use the same [route] every year.
Some young birds make their first journey alone. How do they know the way? Scientists think they are born with an [instinct]. It tells them where to fly.
Every fall, millions of birds leave the places where they live and fly to warmer parts of the world. Every spring, they fly back again. When birds travel like this each year, we say they [migrate].

Why do they do it? In winter, the weather gets cold, and it is hard to find insects, seeds, and other food. So the birds fly to places where food is easier to find. In spring, they return to build nests and raise their babies.

For some birds, the [journey] is amazingly long. The Arctic tern flies from the far north of the world to the far south and back again every year. So how do birds find their way across oceans and mountains without getting lost?
Scientists have found that birds use many different tools. During the day, many birds use the sun to know which direction to fly. At night, many birds use the stars.
Birds can also sense the Earth’s [magnetic field]. People cannot feel it, but for birds it works a little like a compass. It helps them know which way is north, even on a cloudy day.
Birds also use [landmarks|landmark], things that are easy to see and remember, like coastlines, rivers, and mountains. Many birds follow the same [route] year after year.
Some young birds make their first journey alone, without their parents. Scientists think they are born with an [instinct] that tells them which way to fly and for how long.

Every autumn, millions of birds leave the places where they spent the summer and set off for warmer parts of the world. Every spring, they make the trip in reverse. Animals that travel back and forth like this with the seasons are said to [migrate].

The reason is simple: food. As winter arrives, the insects, seeds, and fruit that many birds depend on become hard to find. Flying somewhere warmer gives them a better chance of surviving. When spring returns, so do they, ready to build nests and raise their young where food will soon be plentiful again.

Some of these trips are remarkable. The Arctic tern, for example, makes a [journey] each year from the far north of the planet to the far south and back again. That raises an obvious question: how do birds cross oceans, deserts, and mountain ranges without getting lost?

The answer is that they rely on several tools at once. During the day, many birds steer by the position of the sun. Many birds that fly at night use the stars instead, learning the patterns of the night sky while they are still young.

Birds can also sense the Earth’s [magnetic field], something people cannot feel at all. For a bird, it works much like a built-in compass, pointing the way north even when clouds hide the sun and stars. Scientists are still studying exactly how birds detect it.
Closer to the ground, birds watch for [landmarks|landmark], features that are easy to spot and remember, such as coastlines, rivers, and mountains. Many return along the same [route] year after year.

Perhaps most surprising of all, some young birds make their first migration completely alone, with no parent to follow. Scientists believe these birds are born with an [instinct] that tells them which direction to fly and roughly how long to keep going.

texts.title: How Does an Octopus Hide?
texts.summary: An octopus can change its color and its skin in less than a second, squeeze into tiny spaces, and shoot out ink.

parts: An octopus lives in the sea. It has eight arms and a soft body. Many animals want to eat it. These animals are [predators|predator].
An octopus has no bones and no shell. So how does it stay safe? It is very good at hiding.
Its skin can change color very fast, in less than one second. It can turn brown, red, gray, or white. It can look just like a rock. It can [blend in] with the sea floor. This is called [camouflage].
The skin can also change its [texture]. It can be smooth. Or it can become bumpy, like a rock.
An octopus can [squeeze] into very small holes, because its body is soft. The only hard part is its beak. The beak is in its mouth.
If a predator finds it, the octopus shoots out dark [ink]. The ink makes a cloud in the water. The predator cannot see. The octopus swims away fast.
The octopus is a sea animal with eight arms and a soft body. Sharks, eels, seals, and many big fish would like to eat it. These hunters are called [predators|predator].
An octopus has no shell and no bones to protect it, so it needs other ways to stay safe. Its best trick is hiding.

An octopus’s skin is full of tiny sacs of color. Small muscles open and close them, so the octopus can change its color in less than a second. It can turn brown, red, gray, or almost white, and it can even make patterns like spots and stripes. This helps it [blend in] with rocks, sand, and plants. Hiding like this is called [camouflage].

The octopus can also change the [texture] of its skin. It can make its skin smooth like sand or bumpy like a rock covered with sea plants. Then it is very hard to see, even when it is right in front of you.

Because it has no bones, an octopus can [squeeze] through very small openings. The only hard part of its body is its beak, a sharp mouth like a bird’s. If its beak can fit through a hole, the rest of its body can follow.

If a predator still finds it, the octopus has one more trick. It shoots out a cloud of dark [ink]. The predator cannot see through the cloud, and while it is confused, the octopus shoots away through the water.

With eight soft arms and no shell, the octopus might seem like an easy meal. Sharks, moray eels, seals, and large fish are all [predators|predator] that hunt it. Yet octopuses survive in oceans all over the world, largely because they are masters of disappearing.

Their most remarkable tool is their skin. It contains thousands of tiny, stretchy sacs filled with color, each one surrounded by muscles. When the muscles pull, a sac spreads open and its color shows; when they relax, it shrinks almost to nothing. Controlled by the octopus’s brain and nerves, these sacs can change its color and pattern in less than a second, letting it [blend in] with rock, sand, or coral. Scientists call this kind of disguise [camouflage].

Color is only half the trick. An octopus can also change the [texture] of its skin, raising small bumps and points so that it looks like a rough, weedy rock rather than an animal. Strangely, most octopuses are thought to be color-blind, and scientists are still working out how they match their surroundings so well.

An octopus has no bones at all. The only hard part of its body is its beak, which it uses to bite and eat. As a result, it can [squeeze] its soft body through a gap not much bigger than its beak, slipping into cracks where predators cannot follow.

When all else fails, it has one last defense. It squirts a cloud of dark [ink] into the water, which hides it and confuses the attacker. While the predator is distracted, the octopus pushes water out of its body like a jet and shoots away to safety.

texts.title: How Do Plants Make Their Own Food?
texts.summary: Plants do not eat. They use sunlight, water, and air to make sugar, and they give us oxygen at the same time.

parts: People and animals eat food. Plants do not eat. They make their own food. How?
Plants use sunlight, water, and air. This is called [photosynthesis].
A plant has [roots|root] under the ground. The roots [absorb] water from the soil, like a sponge. The water goes up to the leaves.
Leaves also take in a gas from the air. It is called [carbon dioxide]. It goes in through very small holes in the leaves.
Leaves are green. They have a green thing in them called chlorophyll. It catches the light from the sun.
The plant uses this light to change water and carbon dioxide into sugar. The sugar is food for the plant. It helps the plant grow. The plant keeps some sugar for later, in its roots, seeds, or fruit.
The plant also [produces|produce] [oxygen]. It lets the oxygen out into the air. People and animals need oxygen to breathe.
So plants give us food and air. When you breathe, you can thank a plant!

You eat breakfast, lunch, and dinner to get energy. But a tree never eats a meal. So how does it stay alive and grow so big? Plants make their own food, and they do it with sunlight. This process is called [photosynthesis].
A plant needs three things to make food: sunlight, water, and air.
First, the plant gets water. Its [roots|root] grow down into the soil and [absorb] water, like a sponge. The water travels up the stem to the leaves.
Next, the leaves take in [carbon dioxide], a gas in the air. It goes in through tiny holes on the leaves. These holes are so small that you cannot see them without a microscope.
Leaves are green because they have a green substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll catches the energy in sunlight.

Inside the leaf, the plant uses this energy to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar. The sugar is the plant’s food. It gives the plant energy to grow. The plant saves some extra sugar for later, in its roots, stems, seeds, or fruit.

Photosynthesis also [produces|produce] [oxygen]. The plant does not need all of it, so it lets the oxygen out into the air. People and animals need oxygen to breathe. So every time you breathe in, you can thank a plant. And when you eat fruit, rice, or bread, you are eating food that a plant made with sunlight.

Every living thing needs food for energy. People and animals get it by eating, but a plant never takes a bite of anything. Instead, a plant makes its own food from three simple ingredients: sunlight, water, and air. Scientists call this process [photosynthesis], from Greek words meaning “putting together with light.”
It is one of the most important processes on Earth. Almost all the food we eat, and much of the air we breathe, depends on it.

The process starts underground. A plant’s [roots|root] spread through the soil and [absorb] water, along with small amounts of minerals. Thin tubes inside the stem carry this water all the way up to the leaves, even to the top of a tall tree.

At the same time, the leaves take in [carbon dioxide] from the air. The gas enters through tiny openings, mostly on the underside of the leaf, that can open and close. They are far too small to see without a microscope.
Leaves get their green color from chlorophyll, a substance that is very good at capturing the energy in sunlight. That is why most of a plant’s food is made in its leaves.

Using the energy from sunlight, the leaf breaks water apart and combines it with carbon dioxide to build sugar. This sugar is the plant’s food. The plant burns some of it right away for energy and uses some to build new leaves, stems, and roots. It stores the rest, often as starch, in places like roots, seeds, and fruit. That is why foods such as potatoes, rice, and wheat give us so much energy.

Photosynthesis also [produces|produce] [oxygen], which the plant releases into the air. Over millions of years, plants and tiny water organisms called algae have filled the air with the oxygen that people and animals breathe. So each time you eat a meal or take a breath, you are depending on photosynthesis.

texts.title: How Does Your Heart Pump Blood?
texts.summary: Your heart is a strong muscle that never rests. It sends blood to your lungs for oxygen and then out to your whole body.

parts: Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel your heart? It works all day and all night. It never stops.
Your heart is a strong [muscle]. It is about the size of your fist.
Your heart is a [pump]. It pushes blood through your whole body. The blood moves in tubes. These tubes are called [blood vessels|blood vessel].
Blood carries [oxygen]. Every part of your body needs oxygen to live.
Inside, the heart has four parts, like four small rooms.
The right side of the heart sends blood to your [lungs|lung]. In the lungs, the blood gets oxygen from the air you breathe.
Then the blood goes back to the left side of the heart. The heart pumps it out to the body. It goes in tubes called [arteries|artery].
The body uses the oxygen. Then the blood goes back to the heart in [veins|vein]. And it starts again.
Small doors in the heart keep the blood moving one way. When they close, they make the sound of your heartbeat.
An adult heart beats about 60 to 100 times a minute. That is about 100,000 times a day! When you run, it beats faster. Exercise helps keep your heart strong.
Put your hand on your chest and stay still. You may feel a steady beat. That is your heart, working day and night, even while you sleep.

Your heart is a [muscle] about the size of your fist. It sits in the middle of your chest, a little to the left. Its job is to work like a [pump]. Each time it squeezes, it pushes blood out into a huge network of tubes called [blood vessels|blood vessel]. These tubes reach every part of your body, from your brain to your toes.
Why does blood need to move? Blood carries [oxygen], and every part of your body needs oxygen to live. Blood also carries food from your meals and takes away waste.

Inside, the heart has four spaces, two on the right side and two on the left. The right side sends blood to your [lungs|lung]. In the lungs, the blood picks up fresh oxygen from the air you breathe in. It also drops off carbon dioxide, a waste gas that you breathe out.
Then the blood flows back to the left side of the heart. The left side is stronger. It pumps the blood out to the rest of your body through large blood vessels called [arteries|artery].
As the blood travels, the body takes the oxygen it needs. Then the blood returns to the heart through [veins|vein], and the trip starts again.

Between the spaces in the heart, there are small doors called valves. They open to let blood through and then close so that it cannot flow backward. When they close, they make the “lub-dub” sound that a doctor hears through a stethoscope.

At rest, an adult’s heart usually beats about 60 to 100 times a minute. That adds up to about 100,000 beats a day. When you run or climb stairs, your heart beats faster to send more oxygen to your muscles. Regular exercise, healthy food, and not smoking all help keep your heart strong.

Place your hand on your chest and sit quietly, and you may feel a steady beat. That rhythm is your heart, and it has been working without a break since before you were born. It will keep going every minute of your life, even while you sleep.

The heart is a hollow [muscle], about the size of a fist, that sits in the middle of the chest, pointing slightly to the left. It works as a [pump]: with each squeeze, it pushes blood into an enormous network of [blood vessels|blood vessel] that reaches every part of the body, from the brain to the tips of the toes.

Blood has to keep moving because it delivers [oxygen], along with nutrients from food, to every cell in the body, and it carries away waste. Without a steady supply of oxygen, brain cells can be damaged within minutes.

The heart is divided into four chambers: two upper ones that receive blood and two lower ones that pump it out. The right side handles blood that has already given up its oxygen. It sends this blood to the [lungs|lung], where it releases carbon dioxide, a waste gas you breathe out, and picks up a fresh load of oxygen.

This oxygen-rich blood flows back to the left side of the heart, which has thicker, more powerful walls. The left side pumps the blood out through large [arteries|artery] to the head, arms, legs, and organs.
Once the body’s cells have taken the oxygen they need, the blood returns to the heart through the [veins|vein], and the whole journey begins again.

Four valves inside the heart act like one-way doors. They open to let blood pass and snap shut to keep it from flowing backward. The closing of these valves creates the familiar “lub-dub” sound that a doctor listens to with a stethoscope.

At rest, a healthy adult heart usually beats between 60 and 100 times a minute, which adds up to roughly 100,000 beats a day. During exercise, it speeds up to deliver extra oxygen to working muscles. Like any muscle, the heart stays stronger with regular activity, and a balanced diet and avoiding smoking help protect it for life.

texts.title: How Does the Moon Cause Tides?
texts.summary: The moon’s gravity pulls on the oceans. As the Earth turns, the sea rises and falls along the shore.

parts: At the beach, the sea moves. For a few hours, the water comes higher up on the sand. Then it goes back down. This is called the [tide].
Why does this happen? The answer is in the sky. It is the moon!
The moon has [gravity]. Gravity is a force. It [pulls|pull] things toward each other. The moon pulls on the Earth and on the ocean.
The ocean water moves toward the moon a little. On that side of the Earth, the water gets higher. The water also gets higher on the other side of the Earth.

The Earth turns around once every day. So at each beach, the water goes up and down. When the water at the [shore] [rises|rise], it is high tide. Most beaches have two high tides and two low tides every day.
The sun pulls on the ocean too. When the sun and the moon [line up], the tides are very big.

If you spend a day at the beach, you will see that the sea does not stay in the same place. For a few hours, the water slowly comes higher up the sand. Then, for a few hours, it moves back again. This rising and falling of the sea is called the [tide].
In most places, there are two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours. But what makes the ocean move like this? The answer is the moon.

Everything in space has [gravity], a force that [pulls|pull] things toward each other. The Earth’s gravity keeps the moon going around us. At the same time, the moon’s gravity pulls on the Earth, and that includes the water in the oceans.

The moon’s pull makes the ocean water pile up a little on the side of the Earth that faces the moon. The water also piles up on the opposite side of the Earth. As the Earth turns, each beach passes through these two areas of high water. When a place moves into one, the water at the [shore] [rises|rise], and it is high tide. When it moves out, it is low tide.

The sun has gravity too, but it is very far away, so its pull on the oceans is smaller than the moon’s. When the sun, the moon, and the Earth [line up], at the new moon and the full moon, their pulls work together. Then high tides are higher and low tides are lower than usual.

In some places, the tide is very small. In others, it is huge. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water at high tide can be more than 15 meters higher than at low tide. People who fish, sail, or walk along the coast always check the tide times.

Spend a whole day on the beach and you will watch the sea change. The water creeps slowly up the sand for about six hours, then slowly pulls back for about six hours more. This regular rising and falling of the sea is called the [tide], and in most coastal places it happens twice a day, arriving about fifty minutes later each day.
People noticed thousands of years ago that the tides seem to follow the moon. In the late 1600s, Isaac Newton explained why: it is a matter of [gravity].

Every object [pulls|pull] on every other object. The Earth’s gravity holds the moon in its path around us, and the moon’s gravity, in turn, tugs on the Earth. Solid ground hardly moves, but the oceans can flow, so the water on the side of the Earth facing the moon is pulled toward it and piles up slightly.

Surprisingly, a second pile of water forms on the far side of the Earth. There, the moon’s pull is weakest, so the Earth itself is pulled toward the moon a little more than that distant water is, and the water is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth spins, each stretch of coast passes through both areas of high water every day. As it does, the sea at the [shore] [rises|rise] to high tide, and in between it falls to low tide.

The sun also affects the tides, though less than half as strongly as the moon, because it is so much farther away. Twice a month, at the new moon and the full moon, the sun, moon, and Earth [line up]. Their pulls combine, producing extra-high and extra-low tides known as spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. When the sun and moon pull at right angles, at the half moon, the tides are weaker.

The shape of the coast matters too. Out in the open ocean, the tide may raise the water by less than a meter, but in narrow bays it can be enormous. In Canada’s Bay of Fundy, the difference between high and low tide can be more than 15 meters, taller than a four-story building. For anyone who fishes, sails, or walks along the coast, knowing the tide times is not just useful; it can be a matter of safety.

texts.title: How Do Volcanoes Form?
texts.summary: Deep under the ground, rock can melt into magma. When it pushes up through the Earth’s crust, a volcano erupts.

parts: A volcano is an opening in the ground. Very hot rock comes out of it. Many volcanoes look like tall mountains.
The outside of the Earth is called the [crust]. It is made of hard rock. It is broken into very big pieces. The pieces move very slowly.
Deep under the crust, it is very hot. In some places, rock [melts|melt]. It becomes hot, thick liquid. This is called [magma].
Magma is lighter than the hard rock around it. So it moves up. It collects in big pools under the ground.
Magma has gas in it, like the bubbles in soda. The gas makes [pressure]. The pressure grows and grows. Then the magma breaks out of the ground. The volcano [erupts|erupt].
When magma comes out, we call it lava. Some volcanoes also send out [ash]. Ash is like very small pieces of rock. It can be dangerous. But later, it makes the soil very good for farms.
A volcano is an opening in the ground where very hot, melted rock comes out. Over many years, this rock cools and piles up. That is why many volcanoes look like tall mountains with a hole at the top.

To understand volcanoes, we have to look under our feet. The outside of the Earth is called the [crust]. It is made of solid rock, and it is broken into giant pieces called plates. These plates move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Below the crust, it is extremely hot. In some places, the rock [melts|melt] and becomes a thick liquid called [magma]. This often happens where two plates pull apart, or where one plate slides under another one. It can also happen over very hot places deep inside the Earth. The islands of Hawaii formed over one of these hot places.
Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises toward the surface, the way oil rises in water. It collects in large pools under the ground.

Magma has gases in it, like the bubbles in a bottle of soda. As more magma collects, the [pressure] grows. When the pressure becomes too strong, the magma breaks through the crust, and the volcano [erupts|erupt].

Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Some eruptions are gentle, and the lava flows out slowly. Others are very powerful and throw huge clouds of [ash] into the sky. Ash can be dangerous, but over time it also makes the soil around volcanoes very rich. That is one reason why many farmers live near volcanoes.

A volcano is, at its simplest, a place where molten rock escapes from inside the Earth. Each time it does, the rock cools and hardens, and over thousands of years these layers can build up into the tall, cone-shaped mountains most of us picture when we hear the word.

To see why volcanoes form where they do, we need to look beneath our feet. The Earth’s outer shell, the [crust], is made of solid rock, but it is not one single piece. It is cracked into enormous plates that drift very slowly, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

Below the crust, temperatures are extremely high. In certain places, rock [melts|melt] into a thick, glowing liquid called [magma]. This tends to happen at the edges of plates: where two plates pull apart, or where one plate is forced down beneath another. Magma can also form above unusually hot spots deep inside the planet, which is how the islands of Hawaii were built, one volcano at a time.

Because magma is lighter than the solid rock that surrounds it, it slowly works its way upward, much as oil rises through water. It gathers in large underground chambers, sometimes for a very long time.

Magma contains dissolved gases, a little like the bubbles trapped in a bottle of soda. As more magma collects, the [pressure] builds. When the rock above can no longer hold it back, the magma forces its way through the crust, and the volcano [erupts|erupt].

Once it reaches the surface, magma is called lava. Some eruptions are quiet, with lava slowly spilling down the slopes. Others are explosive, blasting vast clouds of [ash] high into the sky. That ash can be deadly, yet over time it breaks down into some of the richest soil on Earth, which is why farmers around the world have long been willing to live in the shadow of a volcano.

texts.title: Looking for Biscuit
texts.summary: When an old man’s little dog runs away, the people in his building finally meet each other.

Mr. Okafor lived on the fourth floor of a big apartment building. He was eighty-one and walked slowly with a cane. His only family in the city was a little brown dog named Biscuit.
Every morning, they went down in the elevator together for a short walk. Mr. Okafor held the [leash] with one hand and his cane with the other.
One Tuesday, just as they came into the lobby, a delivery man pushed the front door open. Biscuit pulled hard, and the leash fell out of Mr. Okafor’s hand. In a second, the dog was gone.
Mr. Okafor couldn’t run. He stood by the door, calling Biscuit’s name. He was so [worried] that his hands were shaking.
Lina, a teenager from the second floor, was on her way to school. She saw his face and stopped. “Don’t worry,” she said. “I’ll help you find him.”

Soon there were ten people in the [search]. A nurse who had just finished her night shift checked the street. A family from Guatemala looked in the parking lot. Even the man with the loud music, who nobody liked, searched every floor of the stairs.
After an hour, Lina walked past the laundry room in the basement. Then she heard a tiny sound: the bell on Biscuit’s [collar]. There he was, asleep on a pile of warm towels.

Mr. Okafor lived on the fourth floor of a tall, tired apartment building at the end of Maple Street. He was eighty-one, walked slowly with a wooden cane, and had no family left in the city except a small brown dog named Biscuit, who was afraid of almost everything.

Every morning at seven, the two of them rode the elevator down for a short walk around the block. Mr. Okafor held the [leash] in his left hand and his cane in his right, and Biscuit trotted beside him like a little soldier.

One Tuesday, just as they stepped into the lobby, a delivery man backed through the front door with a stack of boxes. A truck horn sounded outside. Biscuit jumped, pulled hard, and the leash slipped out of Mr. Okafor’s fingers. In a second, the dog had disappeared.
Mr. Okafor couldn’t run, not anymore. He stood in the doorway calling “Biscuit! Biscuit!” into the cold air. He was so [worried] that his hands shook on his cane.

Lina, a fifteen-year-old from the second floor, was hurrying out to catch her school bus. She saw the old man’s face and stopped. The bus could wait. “Don’t worry, Mr. Okafor,” she said, although she had never spoken to him before. “I’ll help you find him.”

She ran up and down the halls and [knocked|knock] on every door she passed. One by one, the [neighbors|neighbor] came out in slippers and work clothes. Most of them had lived in the building for years, but they hardly knew one another’s names.

Within twenty minutes, ten people had joined the [search]. A nurse who had just come home from her night shift checked the sidewalks. A family from Guatemala, with two small children, looked under every car in the parking lot. Even the man in 3C, whose loud music had made everyone angry for months, searched the stairs from top to bottom.

After an hour, Lina was walking past the laundry room in the basement when she heard a tiny, familiar sound: the bell on Biscuit’s [collar]. There he was, curled up on a pile of warm towels someone had left on a dryer, fast asleep.

The whole group laughed, and Mr. Okafor cried a little, holding the dog against his chest. Things are different in the building now. People say hello in the hallway and hold the elevator for each other. And every Saturday afternoon, a few neighbors drink tea in Mr. Okafor’s small apartment, with Biscuit asleep on someone’s feet. Even the man in 3C comes, and he turns his music down.
