texts.title: Notes on the Door
texts.summary: A young man is annoyed by the notes his downstairs neighbor leaves, until the notes stop.

parts: Yusuf moved into a small apartment on the second floor. On his first night, he came home late. The front door was heavy, and it [slammed|slam] behind him.
In the morning, there was a note on his door. It said, “Please close the door softly at night. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf was [annoyed]. He did not even know her! He threw the note away.
But more notes came. “The trash goes out on Tuesday.” “Your box is with me.” They all had the same neat [handwriting].
Sometimes Yusuf saw Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]. She was small, with gray hair.
One day, Yusuf wrote a note back. He was [polite]. “Thank you for keeping my box. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next day, she wrote, “You’re welcome. You work too late. Eat something.”
After that, they wrote notes almost every day. Mrs. Ortiz told him about the buses. Yusuf told her about his job.
Then, for one week, there were no notes. Yusuf was worried. He knocked on her door.
Mrs. Ortiz opened it slowly. She was sick, and she lived alone. Yusuf understood. She was [lonely]. The notes were her way to talk to someone.
Yusuf brought her soup. The next day, he put a note on her door: “Call me if you need anything. I am right upstairs.”

When Yusuf moved into his first apartment in the city, he didn’t know anyone in the building. On his first night, he came home late from work. The front door was heavy, and it [slammed|slam] shut behind him.
The next morning, there was a note taped to his door. “Please close the door gently after 10 p.m. Some of us go to bed early. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf was [annoyed]. Why didn’t she just knock and tell him? He folded the note and threw it away.

But the notes kept coming. “Trash goes out on Tuesday night, not Wednesday.” “The mailman left your box with me.” “Watch the third step. It’s loose.” They were always written in the same neat, careful [handwriting].
Sometimes he saw Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]. She was a small woman with gray hair, and she always carried a bag of groceries.

One day, Yusuf decided to write back. He kept it short and [polite]: “Thank you for keeping my box. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next morning, a new note said, “You’re welcome. You work too late. Eat something.”
After that, they wrote to each other almost every day. She told him which bus was fastest. He told her about his new job and the town he came from.
Then, one week, there were no notes at all. Yusuf checked his door every morning. On the fifth day, he went downstairs and knocked.

Mrs. Ortiz opened the door slowly. She had been sick with the flu, and she had no family nearby. In the quiet apartment, Yusuf understood that she was [lonely]. The notes were her way of talking to someone.

That evening, he brought her soup from the corner store. The next morning, he taped a new note to her door: “If you need anything, call me. I’m right upstairs.” He wrote his phone number under his name.

When Yusuf moved into his first apartment in the city, he did not know a single person in the building, and he planned to keep it that way. He worked long hours at a warehouse across town and wanted nothing more than a quiet place to sleep. On his first night, he came home after eleven. The old front door was heavier than it looked, and it [slammed|slam] behind him with a bang that echoed up the stairs.
The next morning, a note was taped to his door at eye level. “Please close the front door gently after 10 p.m. Some of us go to bed early. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf read it twice and felt [annoyed]. If she had a problem, why couldn’t she just knock and say so? He crumpled the note and dropped it in the trash.

But the notes did not stop. “Trash goes out Tuesday night, not Wednesday.” “The mailman left your box with me. Knock anytime.” “Careful on the third step. It’s loose, and the landlord is slow.” Each one was written on the same small yellow paper, in neat, old-fashioned [handwriting] that leaned to the right.

Now and then he passed Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]: a tiny woman with silver hair, always carrying a grocery bag that looked too heavy for her. She nodded at him. He nodded back. Neither of them said a word.

Finally, mostly because he wanted his box, Yusuf wrote back. He kept it short and [polite]: “Thank you for keeping my package. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next morning, the reply was waiting: “You’re welcome. You come home too late. Eat something green.” He laughed out loud in the empty stairwell.

After that, the notes went back and forth almost every day. She told him which bus was fastest in the rain and which bakery sold yesterday’s bread for half price. He told her about the warehouse, and about the mountains outside the town where he grew up. Without quite noticing, he started to look forward to the yellow paper on his door.
Then, one week, there was nothing. Monday, no note. Tuesday, no note. By Friday, Yusuf could not stop thinking about the loose step and the heavy grocery bags. He went downstairs and knocked on 1B.

It took a long time for the door to open. Mrs. Ortiz stood there in a thick sweater, pale and coughing. She had been sick with the flu all week, and her only son lived three states away. Looking past her into the silent apartment, Yusuf finally understood. She was [lonely]. The notes had never really been about the door.

That evening, he brought her chicken soup and orange juice from the corner store. The next morning, he taped his own note to her door, on a piece of yellow paper she had given him: “If you need anything, call me. I’m right upstairs.” Under his name, he wrote his phone number, in his very best handwriting.

texts.title: Plot Seventeen
texts.summary: A man with no yard gets a small piece of a community garden, and his plants are not doing well.

parts: Farid was sixty-two. He lived in a small apartment. He had no yard.
When he was a boy, his father had a big garden. Farid missed the smell of tomatoes and mint.
One spring, he got a [plot] in the community garden. It was number seventeen.
He bought many [seeds|seed]. He put them all in the [soil], very close together. He watered them every morning and every evening.
Next to him was plot eighteen. An older woman named Carmen worked there. Her plants were tall and green. She did not talk much.
By June, Farid’s plants were small and yellow. He did not understand why.
One morning, Carmen came over. She touched his soil. “Too much water,” she said. “And too close. Plants need space. And [patience].”
Farid listened to her [advice]. He gave the plants less water. He took out some small plants. Slowly, the others grew.
In August, it was time to [harvest]. Farid had too many cucumbers. Carmen had too many peppers. So they traded.
Now they talk every morning. Carmen teaches him Spanish words. He teaches her Farsi words. Together, they learn English words for plants.
Farid was sixty-two and lived in a small apartment on the fifth floor. He had a window, but no yard.

When he was a boy, his father had a big garden behind their house. Farid still remembered the smell of tomatoes and fresh mint in the summer. In his new country, he missed that smell more than he could say.
One spring, his name came up on the waiting list, and he got a [plot] in the community garden near the library. It was number seventeen, a small square of dirt between two paths.
Farid was excited. He bought twelve packets of [seeds|seed] and planted all of them in the [soil] in one afternoon, very close together. Then he watered them every morning and every evening.
The plot next to his, number eighteen, belonged to an older woman named Carmen. Her tomatoes were tall, and her peppers were shiny and green. She nodded at him, but she didn’t say much.
By June, Farid’s plants were short and yellow. Some of them were already dying. He didn’t understand what he was doing wrong.
One morning, Carmen stepped over the little fence. She pushed her fingers into his soil and shook her head. “Too much water,” she said. “And too close. Plants need space. And [patience].”
Farid followed her [advice]. He watered less and pulled out some of the smaller plants so the others had room. Slowly, the leaves turned green again.
In August, it was time to [harvest]. Farid had more cucumbers than he could eat, and Carmen had a mountain of peppers. So they traded, a bag for a bag.
Now they talk every morning. Carmen teaches him Spanish words, and he teaches her words in Farsi. Together, they are learning the English names for everything that grows.

Farid was sixty-two and lived in a small apartment on the fifth floor of a building with a broken elevator. He had one window that looked out at a parking lot, and on it he kept a single pot of basil that never seemed happy.

When he was a boy, his father had grown a big garden behind their house. Farid could still close his eyes and smell it: tomatoes warm from the sun, fresh mint, wet earth after the evening watering. In his new country, he had found work, an apartment and a few friends, but he had never found that smell again.

So when his name finally came up on the waiting list, after two years, he read the email three times. He had a [plot] in the community garden behind the public library. It was number seventeen, a small square of dirt between two gravel paths, and it was his.

Farid was so excited that he bought twelve packets of [seeds|seed] in one trip: tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, mint, eggplant and more. He planted all of them in the [soil] in a single afternoon, very close together, so that not one inch was wasted. Then he watered them every morning before work and every evening after.

The plot next to his, number eighteen, belonged to an older woman named Carmen. Her garden looked like a picture in a magazine. Her tomatoes were taller than she was, and her peppers were shiny and green. She nodded at him each morning, but she didn’t say much, and Farid was a little afraid of her.
By June, his own plants were short, pale and yellow. Some had already fallen over. He read about gardening on his phone at night, but the more he read, the less he understood what he was doing wrong.

One morning, Carmen stepped over the little wire fence between their plots without asking. She pushed her fingers deep into his soil, rubbed it between them, and shook her head. “Too much water,” she said. “And too close. Plants need space.” She tapped her chest. “And [patience].”

It was hard to hear, but Farid followed her [advice]. He watered every second day instead of twice a day. With a heavy heart, he pulled out half of the smaller plants so the others had room to breathe. For a week nothing happened. Then, slowly, the leaves turned green again.

By August, it was time to [harvest]. Farid had more cucumbers than he could eat in a year, and Carmen had a mountain of peppers she couldn’t give away fast enough. So they traded, a bag for a bag, and then another bag, and then a jar of her pickled peppers for a dish of his cucumber salad.

Now they talk every morning, in a mix of three languages. Carmen teaches him Spanish words, and he teaches her words in Farsi. Together, standing at the fence with dirt on their hands, they are learning the English names for everything that grows.

texts.title: Spring Rolls for the Potluck
texts.summary: A shy cook brings his mother’s spring rolls to a neighborhood potluck, and at first nobody touches them.

parts: Thanh lived alone on Maple Street. He was a good cook, but he was very [shy]. He did not talk much to his neighbors.
One day, he found a flyer on his door. It said: “Neighborhood [potluck]! Saturday at Maple Park. Bring a [dish] to share.”
Thanh wanted to go. On Saturday morning, he made forty spring rolls. It was his mother’s [recipe].
But at the park, he felt [nervous]. The other people brought pasta, chips and cookies. Nobody took his spring rolls. After half an hour, Thanh wanted to go home.
Then a little girl took one. She ate it fast. “Mom!” she shouted. “These are so good!”
Soon, everyone wanted a spring roll. In twenty minutes, his tray was empty.
People gave him many [compliments|compliment]. A woman named Mrs. Okafor asked, “Can I have the recipe?”
Thanh’s face was red, but he smiled. He wrote the recipe on a napkin for her.
At the end, Mrs. Okafor said, “Come next time. And bring spring rolls!” Thanh walked home happy. Now he knew some of his neighbors by name.
Thanh lived alone on Maple Street. He was a very good cook, but he was also very [shy]. When he saw his neighbors, he nodded and smiled, but he almost never talked to them.
One evening, he found a yellow flyer on his door. “Neighborhood [potluck]!” it said. “Saturday at 1:00 at Maple Park. Bring a [dish] to share.”
Thanh read the flyer three times. He wanted to go. Maybe it was a good way to meet people.
On Saturday morning, he made forty spring rolls. It was his mother’s [recipe], with pork, carrots and glass noodles. He fried them until they were golden and put them on a big tray.

But at the park, he felt [nervous]. The long table was full of pasta salad, chips, hot dogs and chocolate cookies. He put his tray at the end of the table and stood near a tree. People walked past his spring rolls. Nobody took one.
After half an hour, Thanh wanted to pick up his tray and go home.
Then a little girl in a red jacket took a spring roll. She ate it in three bites. “Mom!” she shouted. “These are so good!”

Soon there was a line at the end of the table. In twenty minutes, the tray was empty. People gave him [compliments|compliment] all afternoon. A woman named Mrs. Okafor asked, “Did you make these? Can I have the recipe?”
Thanh’s face turned red, but he smiled. He wrote the recipe on a napkin for her, step by step.
When the potluck ended, Mrs. Okafor said, “You have to come next time. And bring spring rolls!” Thanh walked home with an empty tray. For the first time, he knew some of his neighbors by name.

Thanh had lived on Maple Street for almost two years, and he could count on one hand the conversations he’d had with his neighbors. It wasn’t that he didn’t like them. He was simply [shy], the kind of shy that made his words disappear the moment someone said hello. So he nodded, smiled and hurried inside.
Cooking was different. In the kitchen, Thanh never felt shy. His hands knew exactly what to do.

One evening in October, he found a yellow flyer taped to his door. “Neighborhood [potluck]!” it said in big letters. “Saturday at 1:00 at Maple Park. Bring a [dish] to share.” He read it three times, then stuck it on the refrigerator, where it looked at him every time he opened the door.

On Saturday morning, he got up early and made forty spring rolls. It was his mother’s [recipe], the one she made for every holiday: pork, carrots and glass noodles rolled tight in thin rice paper, then fried until golden and crisp. He arranged them on his biggest tray with a small bowl of dipping sauce in the middle.

At the park, his courage started to leave him. The long folding table was already crowded with pasta salad, bags of chips, hot dogs and a mountain of chocolate cookies. Thanh felt [nervous]. His spring rolls suddenly looked strange and out of place. He set the tray down at the far end of the table and went to stand under a tree.

People walked past. They looked at the tray, then reached for the chips. Half an hour went by, and not one spring roll was gone. Thanh began to plan how he could pick up the tray and leave without anyone noticing.

That was when a little girl in a red jacket reached up and took one. She ate it in three quick bites, then turned around with her mouth still full. “Mom!” she shouted across the grass. “These are so good!”

It was like someone had opened a door. Her mother tried one, then the man next to her, then the man’s teenage sons. Soon there was a line at Thanh’s end of the table, and within twenty minutes the tray was empty except for a few drops of sauce. All afternoon, people came over to give him [compliments|compliment]. A tall woman named Mrs. Okafor asked, “Did you really make these yourself? Would you give me the recipe?”
Thanh’s face went hot and red, but he smiled. He borrowed a pen and wrote the whole recipe on a paper napkin, step by step, while Mrs. Okafor asked questions.

As people were folding up the tables, she called after him. “You have to come next time,” she said. “And don’t you dare bring anything but spring rolls!” Thanh walked home carrying an empty tray. For the first time since he had moved to Maple Street, he knew some of his neighbors by name.

texts.title: The Story of the Bicycle
texts.summary: The first bicycle had no pedals. It took almost 70 years to get the bike we know today.

parts: The first bicycle was [invented|invent] in 1817 in Germany. A man named Karl Drais made it.
It was made of wood. It had two wheels but no [pedals|pedal]. You sat on it and pushed the ground with your feet.
You had to keep your [balance] on two wheels.
In the 1860s, people in France put pedals on the front wheel. But the ride was very bumpy.
Later, some bikes had a very big front wheel. They were fast, but people often fell off.
In 1885, a new bike came. Its two wheels were about the same size. A [chain] turned the back wheel. Soon bikes also had soft [tires|tire] filled with air.
The bicycle gave people [freedom]. They could travel far without a horse. Many women rode bikes to go places on their own.
Today, millions of people ride bicycles to work, to school or just for fun. But the first bicycle looked very different from the bikes we ride now.

It was [invented|invent] in 1817 by Karl Drais, a German inventor. It was made of wood and had two wheels, but no [pedals|pedal]. The rider sat on a seat and pushed against the ground with their feet, like walking or running. People called it a “running machine.” Riders learned to keep their [balance] on two wheels.

In the 1860s, people in France added pedals to the front wheel. Now riders could keep their feet off the ground. But the wheels were made of wood and iron, and the roads were rough, so the ride was very bumpy. Some people called these bikes “boneshakers.”

In the 1870s, a new kind of bike became popular. It had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. A bigger wheel went farther with each turn of the pedals, so these bikes were fast. But the rider sat very high, and falls were common and dangerous.

In 1885, an English inventor named John Kemp Starley built a much safer bike. Its two wheels were about the same size, and the rider sat lower. The pedals turned a [chain], which turned the back wheel. Most bikes today still work this way.
A few years later, rubber [tires|tire] filled with air made riding much smoother and more comfortable.
By the 1890s, bicycles were everywhere. They cost less than a horse and were easier to take care of. For the first time, many working people could travel far from home on their own.
The bicycle brought a special kind of [freedom] to women. Many women rode bikes to work, to visit friends or to explore. Some even changed the way they dressed so they could ride more easily.

Today, the bicycle is so familiar that it is easy to forget it had to be [invented|invent] at all. Yet the bike we know took decades of experiments, and some of the early designs would surprise a modern rider.

The story usually begins in 1817 with Karl Drais, a German inventor. His machine had two wooden wheels, a seat and handlebars for steering, but no [pedals|pedal]. Riders moved by pushing against the ground with their feet, taking long, gliding steps. It was nicknamed the “running machine,” and it proved something important: a person could keep their [balance] on two wheels in a line, as long as they kept moving.

In the 1860s, French makers attached pedals directly to the front wheel. Riders could finally lift their feet off the ground, but the iron-rimmed wheels and rough roads made every trip a jolting experience, which is why many people called these machines “boneshakers.”

The 1870s brought the high-wheeler, often called the penny-farthing in Britain. Because the pedals were fixed to the front wheel, a larger wheel meant more distance with every turn, so designers made the front wheels enormous. These bikes were fast and fashionable, but riders sat high above the ground, and a small bump could throw them over the handlebars.

The real turning point came in 1885, when English inventor John Kemp Starley introduced the Rover. With two wheels of similar size and a lower seat, it was far safer. Instead of turning the front wheel directly, the pedals drove a [chain] connected to the back wheel, a design still used on most bicycles today.
A few years later, John Boyd Dunlop developed practical air-filled rubber [tires|tire]. Riding became smoother, faster and much more comfortable, and the modern bicycle was more or less complete.
The result was a bicycle boom in the 1890s. Bikes were cheaper to own than horses, and they let ordinary working people travel farther than ever before, on their own schedule.

For many women, the bicycle meant a new kind of [freedom]. They could go out alone, visit friends or explore the countryside without asking anyone for a ride. Long, heavy skirts were hard to ride in, so some women began wearing shorter skirts or loose trousers, a change that shocked some people at the time. More than a century later, the bicycle is still one of the simplest and most efficient ways to get around.

texts.title: The Story of the Light Bulb
texts.summary: For most of history, people lit the night with fire. Then inventors learned how to make a thin thread glow with electricity.

parts: Long ago, there were no light bulbs. At night, people used candles and oil lamps. Later, some cities had gas lamps on the streets. These lights used fire. They were not very bright, and they could start fires.
In the 1800s, people started to use [electricity]. Many [inventors|inventor] wanted to make a light with it.
They had an idea. Send electricity through a very thin thread. The thread gets very hot, and it starts to [glow]. This thread is called a [filament].
But there was a problem. The filament burned up very fast. Why? There was air in the bulb. So the inventors took the air out of the glass bulb. Then the filament lasted longer.
Two men made good light bulbs at about the same time. Joseph Swan worked in England. Thomas Edison worked in the United States. This was around 1880.
Edison’s team did many [experiments|experiment]. They tried many materials for the filament. A material made from bamboo worked well.
So who [invented|invent] the light bulb? No one did it alone. Many people worked on it. Edison also helped bring electricity into homes.
Today, we have LED bulbs. They use much less electricity, and they last much longer.

For most of human history, the night was dark. People used candles and oil lamps to see. In the 1800s, many cities began to use gas lamps on the streets. But all of these lights used fire. They were not very bright, they made smoke, and they could start dangerous fires.
In the 1800s, scientists were learning more and more about [electricity]. Many [inventors|inventor] wanted to use it to make light that was safe, bright, and cheap.

Their idea was simple. If you send electricity through a very thin thread, the thread gets so hot that it starts to [glow]. This thin thread is called a [filament]. The hard part was making a filament that did not burn up in a few minutes.
Early filaments burned out quickly because there was air inside the bulb. Inventors learned to pump most of the air out of the glass bulb. Without air, the filament could glow for much longer.

Around 1880, two inventors made light bulbs that really worked. In England, Joseph Swan showed his bulb to the public. In the United States, Thomas Edison and his team did thousands of [experiments|experiment] to find the best material for the filament. They found that a filament made from bamboo could glow for a long time.

So who [invented|invent] the light bulb? The truth is that no one did it alone. Many people worked on it, and each one learned from the others. Edison also helped build power stations to bring electricity into homes.
Light bulbs are still changing today. Most new bulbs are LEDs. They use much less electricity than the old bulbs, and they can last for many years.

For most of human history, darkness arrived with the sunset. People lit their homes with candles and oil lamps, and in the 1800s many cities added gas lamps along their streets. Every one of these lights depended on an open flame. They were dim, they filled rooms with smoke, and they caused countless fires.

During the 1800s, scientists were rapidly learning how to produce and control [electricity], and [inventors|inventor] in several countries began to wonder whether it could give the world a light that was brighter, safer, and cheaper than fire.

The basic idea was straightforward. When electricity passes through a very thin thread of material, the thread heats up until it begins to [glow]. This thread is known as a [filament]. The challenge was finding a filament that would not burn away within minutes.

Part of the problem was the air. Inside a bulb full of air, a hot filament quickly burned out. Inventors discovered that if they pumped most of the air out of the glass bulb, the filament could shine far longer.

By around 1880, two inventors had produced bulbs that truly worked. In England, Joseph Swan demonstrated his lamp to the public. In the United States, Thomas Edison and his team ran thousands of [experiments|experiment], testing material after material for the filament, and found that carbonized bamboo could glow for a long time.

So who really [invented|invent] the light bulb? The honest answer is that no single person did. Dozens of people contributed ideas, each building on the work of others. Edison’s larger achievement may have been helping to build the power stations and wiring that brought electricity into ordinary homes.
The story is not over. Today, most new bulbs are LEDs, which use far less electricity than the old glowing filaments and can last for many years.

texts.title: The Story of the Olympic Games
texts.summary: The Olympics began in ancient Greece about 2,800 years ago. They stopped for 1,500 years, then came back in 1896.

parts: The Olympic Games are a very big sports event. The best [athletes|athlete] in the world come to [compete].

The Games started in [ancient] Greece, about 2,800 years ago. Old records say the first Games were in 776 BC, in a place called Olympia. They were part of a festival for the god Zeus. They happened every four years.
At first, there was only one race. Later, there was wrestling, boxing, and horse races too. Only men could compete.
There was a special promise. People could travel to the Games safely, even in a war.
Winners did not get [medals|medal]. They got a crown of olive leaves. They became famous at home.
The old Games went on for more than 1,000 years. They ended around the year 393.
About 1,500 years later, a man from France, Pierre de Coubertin, wanted to [revive] the Games. He wanted sports to bring young people from different countries together in peace.
In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games were in Athens, Greece. Athletes came from 14 countries.
Women first competed in 1900. The first Winter Games were in 1924.

Today, a different city [hosts|host] the Games each time. Athletes come from more than 200 countries. Winners get gold, silver, and bronze medals. The five Olympic rings show the parts of the world coming together.

Every few years, the best [athletes|athlete] in the world meet to [compete] in the Olympic Games. Millions of people watch on TV. But the Olympics did not start with TV, or even with modern countries. They started in [ancient] Greece, about 2,800 years ago.

According to old records, the first Olympic Games took place in 776 BC in Olympia, a place in southern Greece. The Games were part of a religious festival for Zeus, the most important Greek god. They were held every four years.
At first, there was only one event: a short running race. Later, the Games added wrestling, boxing, horse and chariot races, and the pentathlon, a contest with five different events.

Only men could compete, and the athletes came from Greek cities all around the Mediterranean Sea. Before each Games, there was a special agreement. It promised safe travel to athletes and visitors going to Olympia, even when cities were at war.
Winners did not get money or [medals|medal]. Each winner got a crown made of olive leaves. Still, winning made an athlete famous, and his home city often gave him gifts and honors.
The ancient Games went on for more than 1,000 years. Historians believe they ended around the year 393, when Greece was part of the Roman Empire.

About 1,500 years later, a Frenchman named Pierre de Coubertin decided to [revive] the Olympics. He hoped that sports could bring young people from different countries together in peace. In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens, Greece. Athletes from 14 countries took part.

Since then, the Games have grown a lot. Women first competed in 1900, and the first Winter Games, with sports on snow and ice, took place in 1924. Today, a different city [hosts|host] the Games each time, and athletes come from more than 200 countries. The winners get gold, silver, and bronze medals, and the five Olympic rings stand for the parts of the world coming together.

Every two years, taking turns between summer and winter, thousands of the world’s best [athletes|athlete] gather in one city to [compete] in the Olympic Games, while huge audiences follow along on their screens. Yet this very modern event began in [ancient] Greece, around 2,800 years ago.

According to ancient records, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC at Olympia, a religious site in southern Greece. The Games were part of a great festival in honor of Zeus, the king of the Greek gods, and took place every four years.

For many years, the only event was a sprint of about 200 meters, the length of the stadium. Over time, the Games added longer races, wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and the pentathlon, which tested athletes in five events, including the discus and the javelin.

The competitors were free Greek men who traveled from cities across the Mediterranean world. To protect them, the Greeks announced a sacred truce before each Games, promising safe passage to athletes and spectators on their way to Olympia, even when cities were at war.

Champions received no [medals|medal] and no prize money at the Games themselves. Instead, each one was crowned with a wreath of olive leaves. The real reward came later: winners became celebrities, and their home cities often honored them with statues, free meals, and other gifts.

The ancient Games continued for more than a thousand years, even after Greece came under Roman rule. Historians generally believe they ended around AD 393, probably when the Roman emperor banned many of the old religious festivals.

Roughly fifteen centuries later, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin set out to [revive] them. He believed that sport could build character and that friendly competition could bring young people from different nations together in peace. In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, with athletes from 14 countries.

From that small start, the Games have grown enormously. Women first competed in 1900, and the first Winter Games, featuring sports on snow and ice, were held in 1924. Each Olympics now takes place in a different city, which [hosts|host] the Games after being chosen years in advance, and athletes arrive from more than 200 nations and teams.
Winners now receive gold, silver, and bronze medals, and the five linked rings on the Olympic flag represent the parts of the world joined together through sport.

texts.title: Stuck in the Snow
texts.summary: Two coworkers who never talk get stuck together on a bus during a snowstorm.

parts: Marta and Dev worked at the same hotel. Marta cleaned rooms. Dev worked at the front desk. They were [coworkers|coworker], but they never talked.
Marta thought Dev was not friendly. He never smiled.
One night in January, there was a big snowstorm. Marta and Dev took the same bus home. On a hill, the bus could not move. It was [stuck].
“We have to wait for the [snowplow],” the driver said. “Maybe two hours.”
The bus [heater] did not work well. Marta was cold. She was [shivering|shiver]. Dev gave her his scarf.
Marta had sweet bread in her bag. Dev had hot tea. They [shared|share] their food.
They talked. Dev was not unfriendly. He was shy. He worried about his English. In India, he was an engineer. Now he sent money to his mother.
“I thought you didn’t like me,” Marta said. Dev laughed. “I thought you didn’t like me!”
At ten o’clock, the snowplow came. On Monday, Dev brought Marta a coffee. Now they eat lunch together every day.

Marta and Dev worked at the same hotel downtown. Marta cleaned rooms on the sixth floor, and Dev worked at the front desk. They had been [coworkers|coworker] for a year, but they had never really talked.
Marta thought Dev was a little cold. He said “Good morning” and nothing else, and he almost never smiled.
One night in January, a big snowstorm hit the city. Marta and Dev got on the same bus home. Halfway up a hill, the wheels began to spin. The bus was [stuck].
“Sorry, folks,” the driver said. “We have to wait for the [snowplow]. It could be two hours.”
The bus [heater] made a lot of noise but very little heat. Soon Marta was [shivering|shiver]. Without a word, Dev took off his scarf and handed it to her.
Marta called her sister to check on her kids. Then she opened her bag. She had two pieces of sweet bread. Dev had a bottle of hot tea. They [shared|share] everything.

As they ate, they began to talk. Dev wasn’t cold at all, Marta learned. He was shy, and he worried about his English. Back in India, he had been an engineer. Now he worked at the hotel and sent money to his mother every month.
“I thought you didn’t like me,” Marta said. Dev laughed. “I thought you didn’t like me!”
The snowplow came at ten o’clock. On Monday morning, Dev was waiting by the staff door with two coffees. Now they eat lunch together every day, and Dev smiles a lot more.

Marta and Dev worked at the same big hotel downtown. Marta cleaned rooms on the sixth floor, and Dev worked at the front desk in a dark suit and a tie. They had been [coworkers|coworker] for almost a year, but in all that time, they had never had a real conversation.

Marta had decided long ago that Dev was a little cold. He said “Good morning” when she passed the desk, and nothing else. He almost never smiled. She figured he thought he was better than the housekeepers.

Then, one night in January, a huge snowstorm hit the city. By the time their shifts ended, the streets were white and empty. Marta and Dev ended up on the same bus, sitting three rows apart. Halfway up the long hill on Fulton Avenue, the wheels began to spin and spin. The bus was [stuck].
“Sorry, folks,” the driver said over the speaker. “Nobody’s going anywhere until the [snowplow] gets here. Could be two hours.” Only five passengers were on the bus, and all of them groaned.

The bus [heater] rattled loudly but gave almost no heat. Marta’s coat was thin, and soon she was [shivering|shiver] so hard her teeth knocked together. Without a word, Dev stood up, unwound his long gray scarf, and handed it to her. Then he sat down in the seat across from her.

Marta called her sister, who was watching her two kids, to say she would be late. Then she dug in her bag and found two pieces of sweet bread she had bought for breakfast. Dev pulled out a bottle of hot tea. In the cold blue light of the bus, they [shared|share] everything.

As they ate, they began to talk, slowly at first and then easily. Dev wasn’t cold at all, Marta learned. He was shy, and he was always worried that his English sounded wrong, so he said as little as possible. Back in India, he had been an engineer. Now he worked nights at the hotel and sent money to his mother every month, and he hoped to get his license here one day.
“All this time, I thought you didn’t like me,” Marta said. Dev laughed so loudly that the driver turned around. “I thought you didn’t like me!”

The snowplow finally came at ten o’clock, its orange lights flashing through the snow. On Monday morning, Dev was waiting by the staff door with two cups of coffee. Now the two of them eat lunch together every day in the break room, and the people at the front desk say Dev smiles a lot more than he used to.

texts.title: Summer Swimming Lessons
texts.summary: The city pool offers summer swimming lessons for children and adults and explains how to sign up.

parts: Summer 2027 Swimming Lessons at Millbrook Community Pool
Do you want to learn to swim? Come to the city pool this summer!
There are classes for children ages 4 to 12. There is a class for adults too. [Beginners|beginner] are welcome.
All of our teachers are [lifeguards|lifeguard]. They keep everyone safe in the water.
There are two [sessions|session]. Each session is two weeks.
Session 1: June 14 to June 24
Session 2: June 28 to July 8
Classes are Monday to Thursday. Each class is 30 minutes. Children’s classes are in the morning. The adult class is at 6:00 p.m.
How to sign up
Sign-up starts on Monday, May 3, at 8:00 a.m. You can [register] on the city website. Or you can go to the Parks and Recreation office.
First, choose a session and a class time.
Next, fill out the form. Write the swimmer’s age.
Then pay. It is $40 for Millbrook [residents|resident]. It is $55 for other people. Do you live in Millbrook? Show a bill with your address.
Is the class full? Put your name on the [waitlist].
Bring a swimsuit and a towel to every class.
Questions? Call (706) 555-0187.

Classes meet Monday through Thursday and last 30 minutes. Children’s classes are held in the morning, and the adult class meets at 6:00 p.m.
How to sign up

First, choose a session and a class time. Next, complete the sign-up form, including the swimmer’s age. Finally, pay the class fee.

texts.title: The Blue Bicycle
texts.summary: A grandfather finds his daughter’s old bicycle in the garage and spends a week fixing it with his granddaughter.

parts: Sofia was eight years old. Every day after school, she went to her grandfather’s house. Grandpa Ilya liked to fix things.
One day, Grandpa found an old bicycle in his garage. It was blue before, but now it was brown and [rusty]. The [tires|tire] were flat.
“This was your mother’s bicycle,” he said. “She learned to ride on it when she was eight, like you.”
“Can I ride it?” Sofia asked.
“Not yet,” Grandpa said. “First, we fix it together.”
Every afternoon, they worked in the garage. Sofia gave Grandpa the tools. She learned their names, like the [wrench].
Grandpa cleaned off the rust. He cleaned the [chain] and gave it oil. He put on new tires.
Sofia wanted to ride it right away. “Is it ready now?” she asked every day. “Good things need [patience],” Grandpa said.
On Friday, they painted the bicycle blue again. Grandpa made the [handlebars] tight.
On Saturday, Sofia got on the bicycle. Grandpa held the seat and ran next to her. Then he let go. Sofia rode to the corner alone!
Her mother watched from the porch. She laughed, but she had tears in her eyes. “That was my bicycle,” she said.
Every day after school, eight-year-old Sofia went to her grandfather’s house until her mother finished work. Grandpa Ilya liked to fix things: clocks, radios, chairs, anything that was broken.
One afternoon in April, he pulled an old bicycle out from the back of his garage. It used to be blue, but now it was brown and [rusty]. Both [tires|tire] were flat, and the seat was torn.
“This was your mother’s bicycle,” he told Sofia. “She learned to ride on it when she was eight, just like you.”
Sofia’s eyes got big. “Can I ride it?”
“Not yet,” Grandpa said. “First, we fix it together.”
So every afternoon, they worked in the garage. Sofia’s job was to hand Grandpa the tools. She learned the names of all of them: the screwdriver, the pliers and the [wrench].
Grandpa scrubbed off the rust with a wire brush. He cleaned the [chain] and gave it oil until it moved smoothly. On Wednesday, he put on two new tires.
Sofia wanted to ride it right away. “Is it ready now?” she asked every day. Grandpa always gave the same answer. “Good things need [patience].”
On Friday, they painted the bicycle blue again. Sofia chose the color: bright blue, like the sky. Then Grandpa tightened the [handlebars] and raised the seat a little.

On Saturday morning, Sofia climbed on. Grandpa held the back of the seat and ran beside her down the street. “Keep pedaling!” he called. Then, very quietly, he let go. Sofia rode all the way to the corner by herself.
Her mother was watching from the porch. She was laughing, but there were tears in her eyes. “That was my bicycle,” she said softly. Grandpa stood in the street, out of breath and smiling.

Every day after school, eight-year-old Sofia walked to her grandfather’s house and stayed there until her mother finished work at the dental office. Grandpa Ilya had been an engineer for forty years, and now that he had time, he fixed whatever anyone brought him: clocks, radios, wobbly chairs, a neighbor’s lawn mower. His garage was full of jars of screws and the smell of oil.

One afternoon in April, he dug something out from behind a stack of boxes and rolled it into the light. It was a child’s bicycle. It had once been blue, but now it was mostly brown and [rusty], the color of old leaves. Both [tires|tire] were flat, and the seat had a long tear in it.
“Do you know whose this is?” Grandpa asked. Sofia shook her head. “It was your mother’s. She learned to ride on it when she was eight years old, exactly like you.”
Sofia’s eyes went wide. “Can I ride it?”
“Not yet,” Grandpa said, wiping his hands on a rag. “First, we fix it. Together.”

So every afternoon that week, they worked in the garage. Sofia’s job was to hand Grandpa the tools, and by Tuesday she knew every one of them by name: the screwdriver, the pliers, the little [wrench] and the big one.

Grandpa scrubbed the rust away with a wire brush, slowly, one small spot at a time. He took off the [chain], cleaned every link and oiled it until it moved as smoothly as a necklace. On Wednesday, he put on two new tires and let Sofia pump them up, which took a long time and made her arms ache.

Sofia wanted to ride it right away. “Is it ready now?” she asked every single day, sometimes twice. Grandpa always gave the same answer, without looking up from his work. “Good things need [patience].”

On Friday, they painted the bicycle blue again. Sofia chose the color herself, a bright blue like the sky on a clear morning. When the paint was dry, Grandpa tightened the [handlebars] and raised the seat a little, because she was taller than her mother had been at her age.

On Saturday morning, Sofia climbed on. Grandpa held the back of the seat and jogged beside her down the street, puffing. “Keep pedaling! Look ahead, not down!” he called. Then, so quietly that she didn’t notice, he let go. Sofia rode all the way to the corner by herself before she looked back and saw him standing far behind, with both hands in the air.

Her mother had come home early and was watching from the porch. She was laughing, but there were tears in her eyes. “That was my bicycle,” she said softly, to no one in particular. In the middle of the street, Grandpa stood out of breath, smiling as wide as Sofia.

texts.title: The Story of the Postage Stamp
texts.summary: Long ago, the person who got a letter often had to pay for it. In 1840, a small stamp changed that.

parts: Long ago, sending a letter was hard. In some old empires, riders on horses carried messages. These [messengers|messenger] worked for kings, not for everyday people.

Later, many countries had a post office. But in Britain, letters cost a lot. The price depended on how far the letter went. Usually, the person who got the letter paid, not the [sender]. Sometimes people said no and did not take the letter.
A teacher named Rowland Hill had an idea. Make letters cheap. Make the price the same for every place in Britain. And the sender pays first.
In 1840, Britain made the first [stamp]. It was called the Penny Black. It cost one penny. It had a picture of Queen Victoria. People paid the [postage] and put the stamp on the letter.
Soon people sent many more letters. People started to use [envelopes|envelope]. Other countries made stamps too.
Today, some people collect stamps. A stamp [collector] may have thousands!
Today, you can send a letter almost anywhere in the world for a small price. But for most of history, it was not so easy.

Thousands of years ago, the kings of Persia and the rulers of Rome had riders who carried messages across their lands. These [messengers|messenger] changed horses at stations along the road, so the messages could travel fast. But this service was for the government, not for ordinary people.

Over time, many countries started a post office that everyone could use. But in Britain in the early 1800s, sending a letter was expensive and complicated. The price depended on how far the letter traveled and how many sheets of paper it had. Usually, the person who received the letter had to pay, not the [sender]. Some people could not pay, so they refused the letter, and the post office got no money.

A teacher named Rowland Hill had a better idea. He said there should be one low price for a letter going anywhere in Britain, and the sender should pay first. To show that the [postage] was paid, people would stick a small piece of paper on the letter.

In May 1840, Britain started selling the first [stamp] in the world that you could stick on a letter. It cost one penny and had a picture of young Queen Victoria. Because it was black, people called it the Penny Black.

The idea was a huge success. Sending letters became cheap, and people began writing many more of them. Because the price no longer depended on the number of sheets, people also started using [envelopes|envelope]. Soon other countries, like Brazil and the United States, made their own stamps.

Stamps also became something people love to collect. A stamp [collector] may keep thousands of stamps from all over the world. And even today, British stamps show a picture of the king or queen but not the name of the country, because Britain was the first.

Dropping a letter in a mailbox is one of the simplest things we do. Yet the system behind it, in which you pay a small, fixed price in advance and your letter can travel almost anywhere, is less than two hundred years old.

Long-distance messages are, of course, far older. About 2,500 years ago, the Persian Empire built a network of roads with stations where riders could change horses, allowing royal [messengers|messenger] to cross the empire in days rather than months. The Romans had a similar service. But these systems carried the government’s mail, not the letters of ordinary people.

By the early 1800s, Britain had a public post office, but using it was costly and confusing. Charges were based on the distance a letter traveled and the number of sheets of paper it contained, and the cost was usually paid by the person who received it rather than the [sender]. Many people simply refused letters they could not afford, leaving the post office with nothing for its trouble.

In 1837, a schoolteacher and reformer named Rowland Hill published a plan to fix the system. He argued for one low price, a single penny, for an ordinary letter going anywhere in Britain, paid in advance by the sender. As proof that the [postage] had been paid, the sender would attach a small printed label with glue on the back.

The government accepted the plan, and on 6 May 1840, the world’s first sticky postage [stamp], the Penny Black, could be used for the first time. It showed the young Queen Victoria’s head on a black background. The reform worked: letters became affordable for working families, and the number of letters sent across the country rose quickly.

There were other changes, too. Since the price no longer depended on the number of sheets, people began putting their letters in [envelopes|envelope], which soon became common. Other countries quickly copied the idea: Brazil issued stamps in 1843 and the United States in 1847.

Almost at once, stamps also became a hobby. Today a stamp [collector] may own thousands of stamps from around the world. And as a reminder of where it all began, British stamps still carry no country name, only a picture of the king or queen.

texts.title: The First Snow
texts.summary: A family from a warm country waits for their first winter, and the father worries about warm clothes.

parts: The Morales family came from Honduras. In Honduras, it is warm all year.
Now they lived in Ohio. It was December. Every morning, the children asked, “Will it snow today?”
Their father, Carlos, was worried. Winter coats were expensive. The children only had sneakers and thin jackets.
One Saturday, Sofi shouted, “Look!” Everything outside was white. It was their first snow.
Javier and Sofi ran to the door in their sneakers. “No!” said Carlos. “It is [freezing|freeze] out there!”
Then someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man next door. He had a big box. In the box were boots, hats, [mittens|mitten] and a red [sled].
“My grandchildren are grown up now,” he said. “You can [borrow] these.”
The children were [delighted]. They played in the snow all morning. Then Carlos went outside too. He began to [shiver], but he laughed and laughed.
The Morales family came from Honduras, where it is warm all year. Last summer, they moved to a small town in Ohio.
Now it was December. Every morning, Javier, who was nine, and Sofi, who was six, ran to the window and asked, “Will it snow today?”
Their father, Carlos, was worried. He had seen the prices of winter coats and boots at the store. The children only had sneakers and thin jackets, and he didn’t know how to pay for everything.
One Saturday morning, Sofi shouted, “Papá, look!” Everything outside was white: the cars, the trees, the street. It was their first snow.
Javier and Sofi ran to the door in their pajamas and sneakers. “No, no, no!” Carlos said. “It’s [freezing|freeze] out there!”
Just then, someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man who lived next door. He was holding a big cardboard box.

“I saw you didn’t have snow things yet,” Mr. Bell said. Inside the box were boots, wool hats, [mittens|mitten] and a red plastic [sled]. “My grandchildren are all grown up now. You can [borrow] these for the winter.”
The children were [delighted]. In ten minutes, they were outside, falling in the snow and pulling the sled up the little hill behind the house.
Carlos watched from the door. Then he put on his thin jacket and went out too. He began to [shiver] right away, but he caught a snowflake on his hand, and he laughed and laughed.
That night, he wrote a thank-you note to Mr. Bell. At the bottom, Sofi drew a picture of a red sled.

The Morales family came from Honduras, where the year has a wet season and a dry season but never a cold one. Last summer, they had moved to a small town in Ohio, because Carlos had found a job at a factory and his cousin lived nearby.

By December, the children could talk about nothing else. Every morning, Javier, who was nine, and Sofi, who was six, ran to the living room window before they even brushed their teeth. “Will it snow today?” they asked, pressing their noses to the cold glass. Their friends at school had told them about snowmen and snowball fights, and they had watched videos until they knew them by heart.

Their father did not share their excitement. Carlos had walked through the winter section of the department store, looked at the prices of coats and boots, and walked out again. His children had sneakers and thin jackets, and the rent and the electric bill came first. Every night he checked the weather on his phone and hoped the snow would wait until his next paycheck.
It didn’t wait. One Saturday morning in the middle of December, Sofi’s voice came from the living room, so loud that it woke the whole family. “Papá! Mamá! Look!”
Everything outside was white: the cars, the mailbox, the trees, the street. The world looked soft and quiet and new. It was their first snow.

Javier and Sofi ran for the front door, still in their pajamas and sneakers. “No, no, no!” Carlos said, catching Sofi by the back of her shirt. “It’s [freezing|freeze] out there! You’ll get sick!” Sofi’s face fell, and Javier looked at his father as if he had cancelled Christmas.

Just then, someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man from next door who waved from his porch every morning but rarely said more than hello. He was standing in the snow, holding a big cardboard box with both arms.

“I noticed you didn’t have any snow things yet,” Mr. Bell said, a little shy. Inside the box were boots in different sizes, wool hats, two pairs of [mittens|mitten] and a red plastic [sled] with a long rope. “My grandchildren are all grown up and live in Texas now. These were just sitting in my garage. You can [borrow] them for as long as you need.”

The children were [delighted]. Within ten minutes, they were outside in boots one size too big, falling backward into the snow, throwing it at each other, and pulling the sled up the little hill behind the house again and again.

Carlos watched from the doorway with Mr. Bell beside him. Then, because he could not stand it any longer, he put on his thin jacket and stepped outside. The cold hit him like a wall, and he began to [shiver] right away. But a snowflake landed on the back of his hand, perfect and white, and before it melted he started to laugh. He laughed until Sofi hit him with a snowball, and then he laughed even more.
That night, Carlos wrote a thank-you note to Mr. Bell, and he invited him for dinner on Sunday. At the bottom of the note, Sofi drew a red sled with four people on it, all of them smiling.

texts.title: The Last Night Shift
texts.summary: After thirty-four years, a nurse works her last night at the hospital and spends it with a patient who cannot sleep.

Mariam and her son, Omid, arrived in the United States in March with two suitcases and one backpack. Omid was seven, and he loved books more than anything. Back home he had a whole cardboard box of them, but there had been no room, and they had left it with a neighbor.

Every afternoon on the way home from his school, they walked past the public library on Elm Street, a red brick building with tall windows. Mariam always slowed down. She wanted to go in. One Saturday morning, Omid simply took her hand and pulled. “Please, Mama,” he said. “Just to look.” So they went inside.

At the front desk sat a [librarian] with short gray hair and reading glasses on a chain. Her name tag said Ms. Carter. Mariam took a deep breath and said the sentence she had practiced in the kitchen the night before: “I would like a library card, please.”
“Wonderful,” Ms. Carter said, as if Mariam had just told her good news. “All I need is a photo ID and some [proof] of your address.”

Mariam had brought everything, just in case. She opened her plastic folder and handed over her passport and an electric bill. It was a [utility bill], the first one ever mailed to their new apartment, with her name printed across the top. Ms. Carter looked at both and nodded. “Perfect,” she said.

She typed for a minute, then handed Mariam a small blue card. “There’s no charge,” she added. Mariam turned the card over in her fingers. It had her name on it, spelled correctly, every letter in the right place. After months of forms with her name written wrong, that small thing felt surprisingly big.

By then, Omid had found the children’s [shelves|shelf]. He came back holding three books about dinosaurs against his chest. Mariam chose a book of easy English stories and a cookbook full of bright photos.
They [checked out|check out] five books in all. “They’re due back in three weeks,” Ms. Carter said. “And come back anytime.”

Before she turned off the light, Mariam slipped the blue card into her wallet, right next to her passport, where she kept the important things.

texts.title: The Song in the Taxi
texts.summary: A late-night taxi driver hears his passenger humming a song from the country he left long ago.

Ruben had been driving a taxi on the night shift for twelve years, and he had come to love the city after midnight: the empty bus stops, the blinking yellow lights, the bakeries just starting to glow. He had left El Salvador twenty years before, and in all that time he had gone back only twice.

Ruben turned off the radio. “Excuse me,” he said. “That song. Where did you learn it?”
The young man sat up, a little embarrassed. “From my grandmother,” he said. “She used to sing it to me when I couldn’t sleep. I never learned the words. I just know the tune.”

His name was Diego. He had been born here, and he spoke English with no [accent] at all, but his grandmother came from a small town in El Salvador, barely an hour from the village where Ruben grew up.

So Ruben sang. He started quietly, shy about his rough voice, and then he forgot to be shy. Diego [hummed|hum] along, and by the time they turned onto Oak Street, he was singing the first verse with him, stumbling over the Spanish.

“I’ll call her first thing tomorrow,” Diego said, grinning. Ruben watched him go inside. Then he drove home through the empty streets with the windows down, singing the whole song from beginning to end, the way his father used to.

texts.summary: An eleven-year-old boy goes with his mother to the doctor to help with English, and it is harder than he thought.

Lucas was eleven, and for most of his life he had been the English speaker in the family. His mother, Lucía, spoke Spanish at home and at work, and she knew only enough English to get through a short conversation, if the other person spoke slowly.

For weeks, she had been having bad headaches. She took pills from the store and kept working, until one evening Lucas found her sitting in the dark kitchen with her eyes closed. The next day, she made a doctor’s [appointment]. That night, she knocked on his door. “Will you come with me?” she asked. “You can [translate] for me.”
Lucas felt proud. He spoke English all day at school, he helped his mother at the grocery store and the bank, and he had once explained a phone bill to his uncle. This would be easy.

The office was small and very clean. The doctor, a woman with gray hair and red glasses, smiled at him as if he were a colleague, and began to ask about his mother’s [symptoms|symptom]. “How often are the headaches? Does light make them worse? Does she ever feel sick to her stomach?”
Lucas turned each question into Spanish, and his mother answered, and he turned the answers back into English. It felt a little like a game. So far, so good.

Then the doctor began to explain what she thought was happening. She talked about “blood pressure” and a “new medication” and “possible side effects.” Lucas knew these words in English, sort of, the way you know the faces of people you’ve never talked to. But he had no idea how to say them in Spanish. He opened his mouth, and nothing came out.

His face grew hot. He felt more [nervous] than he ever had before a test. What if he told her the wrong amount of medicine? What if he forgot something important? This wasn’t the grocery store or a phone bill. This was his mother’s health.
His mother saw his face. Without a word, she reached under the table and held his hand.

The doctor noticed too. She put her pen down. “We have an [interpreter] on the phone,” she said gently. “It’s free, and it’s their job. Would that help?” Lucas nodded so fast that his mother almost laughed.

A minute later, a calm voice began to speak Spanish through the phone on the desk. His mother sat up straighter. She asked question after question, more than Lucas had ever heard her ask a doctor, and she wrote the answers on a piece of paper. Lucas just sat beside her and listened.

Outside, in the parking lot, she pulled him into a long hug. “You were very [brave] in there,” she said. “But that was too much to put on you. Next time, I’ll ask for the interpreter myself.” She squeezed his hand. “You can just come and hold my hand.”

texts.title: The Wrong Number
texts.summary: An older woman calls the wrong number and finds a new friend on the other end.

parts: Rosa was seventy years old. She lived alone in Chicago. Every Sunday, she called her son in Texas.
One Sunday, she [dialed|dial] his number. A young man answered. It was not her son. Rosa pressed a wrong number.

Rosa was seventy years old and lived alone in a small apartment in Chicago. Every Sunday at four o’clock, she called her son in Texas. It was the best part of her week.
One cold Sunday, she put on her glasses and [dialed|dial] his number. The phone rang three times. Then a young man answered. “Hello?”
It was not her son. Rosa looked at the paper in her hand. She had pressed a 7 instead of a 1.
“Oh, I’m so sorry,” she said. She [apologized|apologize] again and got ready to [hang up].
“Please, it’s no problem,” the man said. He had a soft, kind [voice]. “My name is Amir. To be honest, nobody has called me all day.”

Rosa was seventy years old and lived alone in a small apartment on the north side of Chicago. Her husband had died three years earlier, and the days were quiet now. Every Sunday at four o’clock, she called her son in Texas. She looked forward to that call all week.
One gray Sunday in November, she put on her reading glasses, picked up the paper with his new number, and [dialed|dial] carefully. The phone rang three times. Then a young man’s voice said, “Hello?”
It was not her son. Rosa looked down at the paper and then at the phone. She had pressed a 7 instead of a 1.
“Oh, I’m so sorry,” she said, her face turning warm. She [apologized|apologize] a second time and was about to [hang up].

“Please, don’t worry, it’s no problem,” the man said. He had a soft, kind [voice], with an accent she couldn’t place. “My name is Amir. To be honest, nobody has called me all day. It’s nice to hear someone.”

Amir, it turned out, was a nursing student from Egypt. He had moved to Chicago in September, and he didn’t know anyone yet except his classmates, who were all busy. He was [lonely], though he didn’t say so. “Sorry,” he added. “My English is not so good.”

Rosa laughed, a real laugh. “When I came from Mexico forty years ago, I couldn’t even order a coffee,” she said. “I pointed at pictures for a whole year. Your English is fine.” They ended up talking for twenty minutes about the cold, about hard tests, and about the food they missed from home.
The next Sunday, Rosa called her son at four, as always. At four-thirty, she dialed the number with the 7 in it. This time, it was not a mistake.

After that, the two of them talked every Sunday. In the spring, Amir passed his big nursing exam, and Rosa baked him a lemon cake to celebrate. He rode the train all the way across the city to pick it up, and he stayed for dinner. One pressed button had turned a [stranger] into a friend.

texts.title: The Wallet on the Bench
texts.summary: A tired man who needs money finds a wallet full of cash at a bus stop.

parts: Daniel worked at a car wash. His rent was due on Friday, and he did not have enough money.
After work, he sat on a [bench] at the bus stop. Next to him was a black wallet. He opened it. There were three hundred dollars inside.
Daniel looked around. No one saw him. He was [tempted]. With this money, he could pay his rent.
Then he looked again. There was a card with a name and an address: Grace Mensah, 14 Hill Road. There was also a photo of a little girl.
Daniel’s bus came, but he did not get on. He walked to Hill Road.
A woman opened the door. Her eyes were red. “Are you Grace?” he asked. “I think this is yours.”
Grace was the [owner] of the wallet. She counted the money. It was all there. She laughed with [relief]. “This is my rent money,” she said.
She wanted to give him fifty dollars as a [reward]. “No, thank you,” Daniel said. “You need it more than I do.”
“You are very [honest],” Grace said. “Then come for dinner on Sunday.” On Sunday, Daniel ate with Grace and her daughter. He had no extra money, but he felt rich.
Daniel finished his shift at the car wash at six. His back hurt, and his rent was due on Friday. He was still eighty dollars short.
He sat down on the [bench] at the bus stop. That’s when he saw it: a black wallet, half hidden next to his leg. He opened it. Inside were three hundred dollars in cash.
Daniel looked around. The street was empty. Nobody had seen him.
He was [tempted]. With that money, he could pay his rent and buy groceries for two weeks. He thought about it for a long time.
Then he looked inside again. There was an ID card with a name and an address: Grace Mensah, 14 Hill Road. Behind the card was a photo of a little girl with a big smile.
Daniel’s bus came, and he let it go. He put the wallet in his pocket and started walking to Hill Road.
A woman opened the door. Her eyes were red, as if she had been crying. “Are you Grace Mensah?” Daniel asked. “I think this is yours.”

Grace was the [owner] of the wallet. She opened it and counted the money with shaking hands. All of it was there. She sat down on the step and laughed with [relief]. “This is our rent,” she said. “I thought it was gone.”
She tried to give him fifty dollars as a [reward], but Daniel shook his head. “You need it more than I do,” he said.

“You’re a very [honest] man,” Grace said. “Then at least come for dinner on Sunday.” That Sunday, Daniel ate rice and chicken with Grace and her daughter. He went home with no extra money, but he felt richer than he had in a long time.

Daniel finished his shift at the car wash a little after six. His back ached, his shoes were wet, and his phone had just reminded him, for the third time that day, that his rent was due on Friday. He was still eighty dollars short, and he had no idea where those eighty dollars would come from.

He dropped onto the [bench] at the bus stop and closed his eyes. When he opened them, he noticed something pressed against his leg: a black leather wallet, worn at the corners. He picked it up and looked inside. Three hundred dollars in twenties stared back at him.
Daniel looked up and down the street. A truck passed. A dog barked somewhere. No one was watching.

He would be lying if he said he wasn’t [tempted]. Three hundred dollars meant rent paid, with enough left over for groceries and maybe new shoes. He could tell himself the owner was probably rich. He could tell himself that anyone would do the same. He sat there with the wallet in his hand for a long time.
Then he looked again. Behind the cash was an ID card: Grace Mensah, 14 Hill Road. Behind that was a small photo of a girl about six years old, missing a front tooth and smiling with her whole face.
Daniel’s bus pulled up, opened its doors and waited. He let it go. He put the wallet in his jacket pocket and started walking toward Hill Road.

It took him twenty-five minutes to find the house. The woman who opened the door looked tired, and her eyes were red, as if she had been crying for a while. “Are you Grace Mensah?” Daniel asked. “I think this belongs to you.”

Grace was the [owner] of the wallet, and she stared at it as if it might disappear again. She counted the money with shaking hands. All of it was there. She sat down right on her front step and laughed, the kind of laugh that comes from pure [relief]. “This is our rent,” she said. “I’ve been looking for it since noon.”
She pressed a fifty-dollar bill into his hand as a [reward]. Daniel gave it back. “You need it more than I do,” he said, and found that he meant it.

Grace looked at him for a long moment. “You’re an [honest] man,” she said. “That’s not so common. If you won’t take money, then come for dinner on Sunday. My daughter will want to meet you.” That Sunday, Daniel sat at a crowded little table, eating rice and chicken while a six-year-old explained the rules of a game he did not understand. He walked home with exactly as much money as before, but he felt richer than he had in years.

texts.title: When the Lights Went Out
texts.summary: A storm turns off the power in an apartment building, and a woman who lives alone knocks on her neighbors’ doors.

parts: It was a hot night in July. A big [storm] came. At eight o’clock, all the lights in the building went out.
Teodora lived alone on the third floor. She was sixty-eight. She knew her neighbors’ faces, but not their names. Sometimes she felt [lonely].
She found a [flashlight] and lit a [candle]. Then she thought about her freezer. It was full of meat and fish. Without power, the food would [spoil].
Teodora had an idea. She took her flashlight and knocked on her neighbors’ doors.
A young couple with a baby opened one door. A tall man with a guitar opened another. A student opened a third. Everyone had food that would spoil.
They took a small grill down to the [courtyard]. They cooked meat, fish and vegetables. The student put candles on the table. The man played his guitar.
At eleven, the lights came back on. Everyone said, “Oh, no!” and laughed.
The next month, there was a note in the hallway: “Courtyard dinner, Saturday at eight. Bring food. No power needed.”
It was a hot night in July when the [storm] came. The wind shook the windows, and at eight o’clock, every light in the building went out at once.

Teodora lived alone on the third floor. She was sixty-eight, and she had lived in the building for five years. She knew her neighbors’ faces from the elevator, but not their names. Some evenings, she felt very [lonely].
In the dark, she found a [flashlight] in the kitchen drawer and lit a [candle] on the table.
Then she thought about her freezer. It was full of chicken, fish and the lamb she had bought for her birthday. Without power, all of it would [spoil] by morning.
She couldn’t eat all that food alone. But maybe she didn’t have to.

Teodora took her flashlight and knocked on the door across the hall. A young couple with a baby opened it. Next, a tall man with a guitar. Then a student who was studying by phone light. Everyone had a freezer full of food that would spoil.

Together, they carried a small grill down to the [courtyard] behind the building. They cooked chicken, fish, lamb and vegetables. The student put candles on the picnic table, and the tall man played his guitar. For the first time, Teodora learned everyone’s names.
At eleven, the lights came back on. Everyone looked up at the bright windows and said, “Oh, no!” Then they all laughed.
The next month, there was a note in the hallway: “Courtyard dinner, Saturday at eight. Bring food. No power needed.”

It was one of those heavy July nights when the air feels like a wet towel, and the [storm] arrived all at once. The wind threw rain against the windows, thunder rolled over the roofs, and at exactly eight o’clock every light in the building went out with a soft click.

Teodora lived alone in apartment 3B. She was sixty-eight and had lived in the building for five years, ever since her husband died. She knew her neighbors’ faces from the elevator and the mailboxes. She knew which ones said good morning and which ones looked at their phones. But she didn’t know a single name, and on some evenings the quiet in her apartment felt so heavy that she turned on the television just to hear a voice. Those evenings, she felt very [lonely].

Now there was no television, no fan and no light. She felt her way to the kitchen, found a [flashlight] in the drawer by the sink, and lit a [candle] on the table. Its small flame made the room look like a different place.

Then she remembered the freezer. It was full: chicken, a big bag of shrimp, and a leg of lamb she had been saving for her birthday. In this heat, without power, all of it would [spoil] long before morning.
Teodora stood in the candlelight and did the math. One woman. Too much food. No way to keep it cold. She couldn’t possibly eat it all alone. But maybe, she thought, she didn’t have to.

She took her flashlight and knocked on the door across the hall before she could change her mind. A young couple opened it, the woman holding a baby who was fascinated by the flashlight. Down the hall, a tall man answered, with a guitar case by his door. At the end, a nursing student who had been studying by the light of her phone. Every single one of them had a freezer full of food and the same worried look.

So they carried a small grill down the stairs to the [courtyard] behind the building, where the rain had stopped and the air smelled clean. They cooked chicken and shrimp and lamb and the young couple’s vegetables, and someone brought out a bag of ice for the drinks. The student lined up candles along the picnic table. The tall man, whose name was Marcus, played old songs, and the baby fell asleep on Teodora’s shoulder. By ten o’clock, Teodora knew every name and two or three stories to go with each one.

At eleven, the lights came back on. All the windows above them lit up at once, bright and ordinary. Everyone looked up, and together, without planning it, they said, “Oh, no!” Then they laughed until the baby woke up.
A month later, there was a note taped to the wall in the hallway, in Teodora’s careful handwriting: “Courtyard dinner, Saturday at eight. Bring food. No power needed.”

texts.title: Why Do Cats Purr?
texts.summary: Cats purr when they are happy, but also when they are scared or hurt. A purr can be a way to talk and a way to feel better.

parts: Many cats make a soft, low sound. It is called a [purr]. You can hear it. You can also feel it when you touch the cat.
How does a cat purr? It uses very small muscles in its [throat]. The muscles open and close very fast. This makes the air [vibrate]. The cat breathes in and out, and the sound goes on and on.
Cats often purr when they are happy and [calm]. But they also purr when they are scared, sick, or hurt. So a purr does not always mean “I am happy.”
Some scientists think purring helps a cat feel better. It may help the cat relax.
A purr is also a [signal]. New [kittens|kitten] cannot see or hear. But they can feel their mother purr. It helps them stay close to her.
Kittens start to purr when they are only a few days old. The purr tells the mother, “I am OK.”
Some cats use a special purr when they want food. They add a high sound, a little like a baby’s cry. It is hard to say no!

If you have ever held a cat on your lap, you may know the sound: a soft, low rumble that seems to come from deep inside its body. This sound is called a [purr]. You can hear it, but you can also feel it with your hand.

For a long time, people were not sure how cats made this sound. Today, scientists know that it comes from tiny muscles in the cat’s [throat]. These muscles open and close very quickly, many times each second. This makes the air [vibrate] as the cat breathes in and out. That is why a cat can purr for a long time without stopping.

Most people think a purring cat is a happy cat. Often, that is true. Cats purr when they are warm, full, and [calm]. But cats also purr when they are scared, sick, or hurt. So a purr does not always mean the same thing.
Scientists think purring may help a cat feel better. It might be a way for the cat to relax, a little like a person who hums a song when they are nervous.

A purr is also a [signal] that cats use to communicate. [Kittens|kitten] are born blind and deaf, but they can feel their mother purr. This helps them stay close to her. Kittens start to purr when they are only a few days old. Their purr tells the mother that they are fine.
Some cats even use a special purr when they want food. They mix a high sound, a little like a baby’s cry, into the purr. Many cat owners find this sound very hard to ignore!

Anyone who has held a cat on their lap knows the sound: a soft, steady rumble that seems to come from somewhere deep inside the animal. We call it a [purr], and it is one of the most familiar sounds in many homes. You can hear it, but you can also feel it, a gentle buzz under your hand.

For centuries, nobody was quite sure how cats did it. Scientists now know that the sound starts with tiny muscles in the cat’s [throat], around the voice box. These muscles tighten and relax many times every second, which makes the air [vibrate] as it moves in and out. Because the sound happens both when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out, a cat can keep purring for a very long time without a break.

Most of us see a purring cat as a happy cat, and much of the time we are right. Cats purr when they are warm, well fed, and [calm]. Yet cats also purr when they are frightened, sick, or injured. A purr, it turns out, does not have a single meaning.

Many scientists believe that purring helps cats comfort themselves. In a stressful moment, it may work a little like a person humming quietly to stay steady. Some researchers are also studying whether the gentle vibration might help a cat’s body heal, though this idea is still being tested.

Purring is also a [signal], one of the ways cats communicate. [Kittens|kitten] are born unable to see or hear, but they can feel their mother purring, and this helps them stay close to her. Within a few days, the kittens begin purring too, letting their mother know that all is well.

Some cats have even developed a special purr for asking for food. Into the usual rumble, they mix a higher sound, a little like a baby’s cry. One study found that people hear this purr as more urgent than an ordinary one, which may explain why so many cat owners end up heading to the kitchen.
