texts.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
texts.summary: In fall, green leaves turn yellow, orange and red. Some of those colors were there all along.

parts: In summer, most leaves are green. In fall, many leaves turn yellow, orange or red. Why?
Leaves make food for the tree. They use sunlight to make sugar. The sugar gives the tree [energy].
A green [pigment] helps the leaves do this. A pigment is a color inside a plant.
In fall, the days get shorter and cooler. The tree stops making the green pigment. The green [fades|fade] away.
Now we can see yellow and orange. These colors were in the leaf all summer. They were [hidden] under the green.
Some trees also make new red colors in fall.
Then the leaves fall from the [branches|branch]. The tree rests in winter. This helps it [survive] the cold.
In many parts of the world, fall is a beautiful time of year. Trees that were green all summer turn bright yellow, orange and red. But why do leaves change color?

The answer starts with food. A leaf is like a small kitchen for the tree. It uses sunlight, water and air to make sugar, which gives the tree [energy]. To do this, leaves need a green [pigment] called chlorophyll. Leaves have so much of it that they look green.
When fall comes, the days get shorter and cooler. There is less sunlight, so the tree slowly stops making chlorophyll. The green color begins to [fade].
As the green goes away, other colors start to show. Yellow and orange pigments were in the leaf all summer, but they were [hidden] by the green. Now we can finally see them.
Red and purple are different. Some trees, like many maples, make new red pigments in the fall. Sunny days and cool nights help make these reds brighter.

Soon after, the leaves fall from the [branches|branch]. This does not mean the tree is dying. In winter, the ground can freeze, and it is hard for a tree to get water. By dropping its leaves, the tree saves water and energy. This helps it [survive] until spring, when new green leaves grow.

Every autumn, forests across much of North America, Europe and East Asia put on a spectacular show. Leaves that were green for months turn gold, orange, scarlet and purple, sometimes all on the same hillside. The change is more than beautiful; it is part of how trees get through the year.

To understand it, start with what a leaf does. Leaves are the tree’s food factories. Using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air, they make sugar that gives the tree [energy]. This process depends on a green [pigment] called chlorophyll. During the growing season, leaves are packed with so much chlorophyll that its green covers every other color.

As autumn arrives, the nights grow longer and the air turns cooler. The tree responds by slowly shutting down its food production. It stops making new chlorophyll and breaks down what is left, and the green begins to [fade].
What remains are yellow and orange pigments, the same kind that give carrots their color. They were in the leaf all summer, [hidden] beneath the chlorophyll. Only now do they come into view.

The reds and purples have a different story. Trees such as many maples actually produce new red pigments in the fall. A run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to make these colors especially bright.

Eventually, a layer of special cells forms where each leaf’s stem meets the [branch], and the leaf breaks off. Losing its leaves might look like a loss, but for the tree it is a way to [survive]. In winter, frozen ground makes water hard to get, and broad leaves would lose a lot of water to the air. By dropping them, the tree saves water and energy and rests until spring, when a fresh set of green leaves appears.

texts.title: Why Does Your Body Need Water?
texts.summary: Water keeps you cool, helps you digest food, and carries what your body needs. Here is why drinking enough matters.

parts: More than half of your body is water. You cannot live long without it. Water has many jobs in your body.
Water keeps you cool. When you get hot, your skin makes [sweat]. The sweat dries on your skin, and you feel cooler.
Water helps you [digest] food. It helps your body break the food down. Then your body can use it.
Your blood is mostly water. It carries [nutrients|nutrient] from your food to every part of your body. Water also takes [waste] out of your body when you use the bathroom.
Water helps your [joints|joint] move well. Your knees and elbows are joints.
Every day, you lose water. If you do not drink enough, you can get [dehydrated]. You may feel tired. Your head may hurt.
So drink water during the day. Fruit and vegetables have water too.

More than half of your body is water. It is in your blood, your muscles, and even your bones. A person can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. Water does many important jobs in your body.

First, water helps you stay cool. When you get hot, for example on a summer day or when you exercise, your skin makes [sweat]. As the sweat dries, it takes heat away from your body, and you feel cooler.
Water also helps you [digest] your food. It helps your stomach break food down into very small parts that your body can use.

Your blood is mostly water. It carries [nutrients|nutrient] from your food to every part of your body. Water also helps your body get rid of [waste]. Your kidneys clean your blood and send the waste out when you use the bathroom.
Water is important for your [joints|joint], too. These are the places where your bones meet, like your knees and elbows. Water helps them move smoothly.

Every day, you lose water when you sweat, when you breathe, and when you use the bathroom. You have to replace this water. If you do not, you can become [dehydrated]. You may feel thirsty, tired, or dizzy, and you may get a headache. Dark yellow urine can also be a sign that you need more water.

The good news is that it is easy to get enough water. Drink water during the day, and drink more when it is hot or when you exercise. You can also get water from food. Fruits and vegetables like watermelon, oranges, and cucumbers are full of it.

Water makes up more than half of the adult human body. It is in our blood and muscles, and even in our bones. A person can survive for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. That is because water is doing important work in almost every part of the body, all day long.

One of its most important jobs is keeping us cool. When we get too warm, whether from a hot summer afternoon or a hard workout, the skin releases [sweat]. As that sweat evaporates, it carries heat away, and our temperature drops.
Water is also essential for helping us [digest] food. It helps the stomach and intestines break meals down into pieces small enough for the body to absorb and use.

Blood is mostly water, and it acts like a delivery system, carrying oxygen and [nutrients|nutrient] from our food to cells throughout the body. Water also helps clear away [waste]. The kidneys filter the blood and remove what the body does not need, sending it out in urine.

Our [joints|joint], the places where bones meet, such as the knees and elbows, also depend on water. The fluid that cushions them is mostly water, and it helps them move smoothly instead of grinding against each other.

We lose water constantly: through sweat, through our breath, and in urine. That water has to be replaced. When it is not, we can become [dehydrated]. Early signs include thirst, tiredness, dizziness, and headaches. Dark yellow urine is another common signal that the body needs more fluid.

Fortunately, staying hydrated is usually simple. Drink water throughout the day, and drink more in hot weather or when you are active. Food helps, too. Many fruits and vegetables, such as watermelon, oranges, and cucumbers, are mostly water, so a healthy meal can also be a refreshing drink.

texts.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
texts.summary: Rivers carry tiny bits of salt to the sea. The salt stays there, and over millions of years it adds up.

parts: Ocean water tastes very salty. River water does not. Why?
It starts with rain. Rain falls on rocks. Little by little, it breaks off very small bits of the rocks. Some of these bits are [minerals|mineral], like salt.
The salt [dissolves|dissolve] in the water. You cannot see it. Rivers carry it to the ocean.
The sun warms the ocean. Some of the water [evaporates|evaporate]. It goes up into the air. But the salt stays in the ocean.
This has happened for millions of years. So now the ocean has a lot of salt. If you took out all the salt, it could cover the land in a thick [layer].
Most rivers and lakes have [fresh water]. It has very little salt.
Do not drink ocean water. The salt makes you more [thirsty].
If you have ever swum in the ocean, you know the water tastes salty. But the rivers that flow into the ocean are not salty. So where does the salt come from?

The answer starts on land. Rain falls on rocks and soil. Over a long time, the rain slowly breaks down the rocks and picks up tiny bits of [minerals|mineral]. Salt is one of them. The salt [dissolves|dissolve] in the water, so you cannot see it.
Streams and rivers carry this water, with its tiny amount of salt, all the way to the ocean. River water has so little salt that we call it [fresh water].

At the ocean, the sun heats the water, and some of it [evaporates|evaporate]. The water goes up into the air and later falls again as rain. But the salt cannot go into the air. It stays behind in the ocean.
Some salt also comes from openings in the ocean floor, where hot water from deep inside the Earth comes up and brings minerals with it.

This has been happening for millions of years. Little by little, the salt has added up. Scientists say that if all the salt in the oceans were spread over the land, it would make a [layer] many meters thick.

Because of all this salt, people cannot drink ocean water. Your body has to use extra water to get rid of the salt, so salty water makes you even more [thirsty]. That is why sailors long ago had to carry fresh water on their ships.

Take a mouthful of seawater and you will not forget the taste. Yet the rivers that pour into the sea every day taste fresh. How can nearly salt-free water from the land end up in such a salty ocean? The answer is a slow process that has been going on for millions of years.

It begins with rain. As rain falls through the air, it picks up a little carbon dioxide, which makes it very slightly acidic. When it lands on rock and soil, it gradually breaks them down, releasing tiny amounts of [minerals|mineral]. Some of these are salts, and they [dissolve] completely in the water, which is why we cannot see them.
Rivers carry these dissolved minerals to the sea. The amounts are so small that we still call river water [fresh water], but every river is always delivering a little more salt to the ocean.

Once there, the salt is trapped. The sun heats the ocean’s surface, and water [evaporates|evaporate] into the air, eventually returning to the land as rain. The salt, however, cannot evaporate. It stays behind, and over time the ocean becomes far saltier than the water that feeds it.
Rivers are not the only source. On the ocean floor, openings called hydrothermal vents release hot water full of minerals from deep inside the Earth, and underwater volcanoes add more.

Most of the salt in the sea is the same kind we sprinkle on our food, and there is a huge amount of it. Scientists estimate that if it could all be removed and spread evenly over the land, it would form a [layer] many meters deep.

All that salt is why seawater is not safe to drink. To get rid of the extra salt, your kidneys have to use more water than the seawater gives you, so drinking it actually leaves you more [thirsty] and can make you seriously ill. For centuries, sailors surrounded by water had to carry fresh water on board.

texts.title: Why Do We Get Hiccups?
texts.summary: A muscle under your lungs makes a sudden jump, and your throat snaps shut. That makes the “hic” sound.

parts: Hic! Hic! Almost everyone gets hiccups. But what are they?
Under your lungs, there is a big, flat [muscle]. It is called the [diaphragm]. It helps you breathe. Most of the time, it moves slowly and smoothly.
But sometimes it jumps. The jump is very [sudden]. Air rushes into your body. Then your throat closes fast. That makes the sound “hic.”
Why does this happen? Sometimes we eat too fast. Sometimes we drink soda. Sometimes we [swallow] too much air. Strong feelings, like excitement, can start hiccups too.
Most hiccups are [harmless]. They stop after a few minutes.
People try many [remedies|remedy]. Some people hold their breath. Some drink a glass of water slowly. These may help, but no one is sure. If hiccups last more than two days, see a doctor.
Almost everyone has had hiccups. They often start for no clear reason, and they can be funny or a little annoying. So what is really happening inside your body?

It starts with the [diaphragm]. This is a large, flat [muscle] under your lungs. When you breathe in, it moves down and pulls air into your lungs. When you breathe out, it moves back up. Usually, you do not even notice it.

A hiccup happens when the diaphragm makes a [sudden] jump that you cannot control. This pulls air quickly into your body. Less than a second later, your vocal cords close tightly, and the air stops. That is what makes the “hic” sound.

Hiccups can start when you eat or drink too fast, drink soda, or [swallow] a lot of air. Feeling excited or nervous can also start them. Even babies get hiccups, and they can have them before they are born.
Most hiccups are [harmless]. They usually go away on their own after a few minutes.

People around the world have their favorite [remedies|remedy]. Some people hold their breath. Others drink a glass of cold water in small sips or eat a spoon of sugar. Scientists have not proven that these tricks work, but they are safe to try. If your hiccups last for more than two days, it is a good idea to see a doctor.

Hiccups arrive without warning. One moment you are talking or laughing, and the next your body is making small, loud “hic” sounds that you cannot stop. Almost everyone gets them, yet few people stop to wonder what causes them.

The story begins with the [diaphragm], a large, dome-shaped [muscle] that sits under your lungs and separates your chest from your stomach. Each time you breathe in, it tightens and moves down, drawing air into your lungs. As you breathe out, it relaxes and rises again. It does this thousands of times a day, usually without you noticing at all.

A hiccup is a [sudden], uncontrolled tightening of the diaphragm, often together with the muscles between your ribs. It makes you pull in a quick breath. A split second later, the vocal cords in your throat snap shut and stop the air. That quick closing is what creates the familiar sound.

Common triggers include eating too quickly, drinking fizzy drinks, and [swallowing|swallow] air, which can stretch the stomach just below the diaphragm. Strong emotions, such as excitement or stress, can set them off too. Hiccups even happen before birth: babies often hiccup in the womb. Scientists are still not sure what purpose, if any, hiccups serve.
The good news is that ordinary hiccups are [harmless] and usually stop on their own within a few minutes.

Every culture seems to have its own [remedies|remedy]: holding your breath, sipping cold water slowly, or swallowing a spoonful of sugar. There is little scientific proof that any of them work, but they are generally safe, and simply waiting is often enough. Hiccups that last longer than two days are rare, and in that case it is wise to see a doctor.

texts.title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
texts.summary: Summer does not come because the Earth gets closer to the sun. The real reason is that the Earth is tilted.

parts: In many places, the weather changes during the year. Summer is hot. Winter is cold. Why?
Some people think it is summer when the Earth is close to the sun. This is not right! The Earth is closest to the sun in January. That is winter in the United States.
The Earth moves around the sun. One trip takes one year. This path is called an [orbit].
The Earth also spins. It spins around a line from the North Pole to the South Pole. This line is called the [axis].
The axis is not straight up and down. It leans to one side. The Earth is [tilted|tilt]. This [tilt] makes the seasons.
The Earth has a north half and a south half. Each half is called a [hemisphere].
In June, the north half leans toward the sun. The sun is high in the sky. The sunlight is more [direct], so it is hotter. The days are long. It is summer.
At the same time, the south half leans away from the sun. It has winter. In Australia, it is summer in December! In spring and fall, the weather is in between.
Near the [equator], the line around the middle of the Earth, it is warm all year. Many places there have a rainy season and a dry season.
In many parts of the world, the year has four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter. Summer brings long, hot days, and winter brings short, cold ones. But what causes these changes?

Many people think it is summer when the Earth is closest to the sun. That sounds right, but it is not true. In fact, the Earth is closest to the sun in early January, when it is winter in the United States. The real reason is the [tilt] of the Earth.

The Earth travels around the sun on a path called an [orbit]. One full trip takes about 365 days, or one year. As it travels, the Earth also spins around an imaginary line that goes through the North and South Poles. This line is called the [axis].

The Earth’s axis is not straight up and down. It is [tilted|tilt] a little, and it always points in the same direction in space. So during part of the year, the northern half of the Earth leans toward the sun. During the other part, it leans away.

Each half of the Earth is called a [hemisphere]. When the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the sun, the sun climbs high in the sky, and its light hits the ground in a more [direct] way. Direct sunlight heats the ground more. The days are also longer, so the sun has more time to warm the land. This is summer.

At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere leans away from the sun, so it has winter. That is why people in Australia and Argentina celebrate the New Year in summer. In spring and fall, neither half leans much toward the sun, so the weather is in between.

Places near the [equator], the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, get strong sunlight all year. They do not have a hot summer and a cold winter. Many of them have a rainy season and a dry season instead.

In much of the world, the year moves through four seasons. Summer brings long, warm days, winter brings short, cold ones, and spring and fall come in between. It is natural to guess that summer happens when the Earth is nearest the sun. It is a popular idea, but it is wrong.

The Earth’s distance from the sun changes only a little during the year, and the planet is actually closest to the sun in early January, in the middle of winter for North America and Europe. The true cause of the seasons is the [tilt] of the Earth.

The Earth travels around the sun in a nearly circular path, or [orbit], that takes about 365 days to complete. At the same time, it spins once a day around its [axis], an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles.

That axis is [tilted|tilt] about 23.5 degrees, and it keeps pointing in the same direction in space as the Earth moves along its orbit. As a result, for part of the year the northern half of the planet leans toward the sun, and six months later it leans away.

Each half of the Earth is called a [hemisphere]. When the Northern Hemisphere is tipped toward the sun, the sun rises higher in the sky. Its rays strike the ground at a steeper, more [direct] angle, so the same sunlight is packed into a smaller area and heats it more. Days are also longer, giving the sun more hours to warm the land. The result is summer.

Meanwhile, the Southern Hemisphere is tipped away. Its sunlight is weaker and its days are shorter, so it has winter. That is why families in Australia and Argentina often spend the New Year at the beach. In spring and fall, neither hemisphere leans much toward the sun, and day and night are close to equal in length all over the world.

Near the [equator], the imaginary line around the Earth’s middle, the sun stays high in the sky all year, so there is little difference between summer and winter. Instead, many of these tropical places have a wet season and a dry season.

texts.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
texts.summary: Sleep is not wasted time. Your brain and body do important work at night.

parts: We sleep for about one third of our lives. Is this wasted time? No! Sleep is very important.
When you sleep, your body rests. But your brain stays busy.
Your brain sorts the things you learned that day. It puts the important things into your [memory].
Your body works at night too. Tired muscles get strong again. Small cuts [heal].
Sleep also helps your body fight [germs|germ].
Without enough sleep, it is hard to [focus]. You may feel sad or angry. Your [mood] gets worse.
Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep. A bedtime [routine] can help. Go to bed at the same time every night. Put your phone away before bed.
Most people spend about one third of their lives asleep. That can sound like a lot of wasted time. But sleep is not wasted at all. While you sleep, your brain and body do important work.
Scientists are still learning about sleep, but they agree on one thing: we cannot live well without it.
Your brain stays busy all night. It sorts through the things that happened during the day. It keeps the important things and puts them into your [memory]. This is one reason sleep helps you learn.
People who sleep well after studying often remember more the next day.

Your body also uses the night to rest and grow strong again. Tired muscles get stronger, and cuts and other small injuries [heal]. Sleep also helps your body fight [germs|germ], so people who sleep too little may get sick more often.
When you do not get enough sleep, it is hard to [focus] on work or school. Small problems can feel big, and your [mood] can change quickly. Tired drivers are also more likely to have accidents.

Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep each night. Children and teenagers need even more. A simple bedtime [routine] can help: go to bed at the same time every night, keep your room dark and cool, and put your phone away before bed.

The average person spends roughly a third of their life asleep. At first, that might seem like an enormous amount of lost time, hours that could be spent working, studying or with family. But scientists now know that sleep is anything but wasted. While your eyes are closed, your brain and body are busy with work they cannot do as well while you are awake.

One of the brain’s main jobs at night is sorting. During the day, it takes in a huge amount of information. During sleep, it replays some of it, keeps what seems important and stores it in long-term [memory], while letting much of the rest fade away.

This is why a good night’s sleep after studying often works better than staying up late. In many studies, people who slept after learning something new remembered it better than people who stayed awake.

Meanwhile, the body takes the chance to recover. Muscles rebuild after the day’s work, small injuries [heal], and the body releases hormones that help it grow. Sleep also supports the immune system, which protects you from [germs|germ]. This is one reason people who regularly sleep too little tend to catch colds more easily.

Missing sleep, even for a night or two, has clear effects. It becomes harder to [focus], make decisions and react quickly. Your [mood] suffers too: tired people often feel more irritable, worried or sad. Drowsy driving is a serious danger on the roads.

Most adults need seven to nine hours a night, and children and teenagers need more. Experts suggest a steady bedtime [routine]: going to bed and waking up at the same times, even on weekends, keeping the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, and putting screens away an hour or so before bed.

parts: NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS
Every year, we check every apartment. This is our yearly [inspection]. Our [maintenance] team will visit your apartment.
Buildings A and B: Tuesday, November 17
Buildings C and D: Wednesday, November 18
Time: from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
The team will test every [smoke detector]. They will put in new batteries if needed.
They will change the [air filter] for your heat and air conditioning.
They will look for [leaks|leak] under sinks and near toilets. They will check your windows and door locks.
The visit takes about 20 minutes.
You don’t need to be home. The team will knock first. No one answers? Then they will use a key to come in.
Do you have a pet? Please put it in a crate or in a closed room.
Do you need a different day? Call the office by Friday, November 13. We can [reschedule] your visit.
Do you need a repair? Tell the team during the visit.
Thank you! Pine Ridge Apartments Office, 555-0164

words.meaning: A person you do not know.

words.meaning: Feeling afraid that something bad has happened or will happen.

words.meaning: The top part of the ground, where plants grow.

words.meaning: Words that tell someone what you think they should do.

words.meaning: To pick fruit, vegetables or other crops when they are ready.

words.meaning: Quiet and relaxed, not worried or excited.

words.meaning: A sound, movement, or sign that gives a message.

words.meaning: A very young cat.

words.meaning: The hard outside layer of the Earth.

words.meaning: The force of something pushing hard against something else.

words.meaning: Water that comes out of your skin when you are hot.

words.meaning: A test you do to find out if something works or is true.

words.meaning: a gas in the air that you cannot see; people breathe it out, and plants take it in

words.meaning: the way something leans to one side and is not straight up and down. If something is tilted, it leans.

words.meaning: one of the tubes in your body that blood moves through

words.meaning: a tube that carries blood from the body back to the heart

words.meaning: one of the two body parts in your chest that fill with air when you breathe

words.meaning: a person who is very good at a sport and trains for it

words.meaning: to bring something back after it has stopped for a long time

words.meaning: to be the place where an event happens and to welcome the people who come

words.short: work, or the cost of the work
words.example: The new part was cheap, but the **labor** cost $200.

words.meaning: A promise from a company to fix or replace something for free if it breaks in a certain time.
words.short: a promise to fix something for free
words.example: My new phone has a one-year **warranty**.

words.meaning: A driving test where you drive a car with a tester to show you can drive safely.
words.short: a driving test on the road
words.example: She passed her **road test** and got her driver’s license.

words.meaning: A car, truck, bus, or other machine that carries people or things on the road.
words.example: Please park your **vehicle** in the back lot.

words.meaning: Something, like a paper, that shows something is true.
words.short: something that shows it is true
words.example: You need **proof** of your address, like a bank letter.

words.meaning: An official paper that shows a car is listed with the state and can be driven on the road.
words.short: the official paper for a car
words.example: Keep your car **registration** in the glove box.

words.meaning: To change the time or day of an appointment or event.
words.short: to change the day or time
words.example: I was sick, so I called to **reschedule** my appointment.

words.meaning: A careful check of something to see if it is safe and working well.
words.example: The fire department does an **inspection** of the school every year.

words.meaning: The work of keeping buildings or machines in good condition, like cleaning, checking, and fixing them.
words.example: Call **maintenance** if your heater stops working.

words.meaning: A small machine on the ceiling that makes a loud sound when there is smoke or fire.
words.short: a machine that warns you about smoke
words.example: The **smoke detector** beeped when the toast burned.

words.meaning: A piece of material in a heating or cooling system that catches dust from the air.
words.short: a part that cleans the air
words.example: Change the **air filter** every three months.

words.meaning: A small hole or crack where water, gas, or air comes out when it should not.
words.short: a place where water comes out
words.example: There is a **leak** under the kitchen sink.

words.meaning: What a test or check shows. Doctors look at the results of a blood test.
words.example: The doctor called me about my test **results**.

words.meaning: The usual way, the way it should be. A normal test result means everything is healthy.
words.example: Your heart rate is **normal**.

words.meaning: Something you do after the first time, to check again. A follow-up visit is a second visit to the doctor.
words.short: a second visit to check again
words.example: The doctor wants a **follow-up** visit in two weeks.

words.meaning: A website or app where you can see your own information and send messages, for example to your doctor.
words.short: a website for your own information
words.example: I paid my bill on the patient **portal**.

words.meaning: To type your name or email and your password so you can open your account on a website or app.
words.example: I can’t **log in** because I forgot my password.

words.meaning: A secret word or set of letters and numbers that you type to open your account.
words.short: a secret word for an account
words.example: Don’t tell anyone your **password**.

words.meaning: Classes or lessons that teach you how to do a job or a skill.
words.short: lessons for a job or skill
words.example: New workers get two days of **training**.

words.meaning: Something you must do or have. It is a rule.
words.example: A photo ID is **required** to open an account.

words.meaning: To finish something, so that all of it is done.
words.example: Please **complete** the form and give it to the front desk.

words.meaning: To stop something bad from happening.
words.example: Washing your hands helps **prevent** colds.

words.meaning: An official paper that shows you finished a class or training.
words.short: a paper that shows you finished
words.example: She got a **certificate** after the first aid class.

words.meaning: The person at work who watches over your work and tells you what to do.
words.example: Ask your **supervisor** if you can leave early.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to watch swimmers and help them if they are in danger in the water.
words.short: a person who keeps swimmers safe
words.example: The **lifeguard** blew her whistle at the boys.

words.meaning: A period of time when a group of classes happens, for example two weeks of lessons.
words.example: The fall **session** of English classes starts in September.

words.meaning: A person who lives in a certain place, like a city or a building.
words.short: a person who lives in a place
words.example: Parking is free for city **residents**.

words.meaning: A list of people who wait for a place when a class or program is full.
words.short: a list of people waiting for a place
words.example: The class was full, so I put my name on the **waitlist**.

words.meaning: a person who rides in a car, taxi, bus, train or plane but is not the driver
words.example: The taxi driver helped the **passenger** with her bags.

words.meaning: to sing a song with your mouth closed, without words
words.example: She likes to **hum** while she cooks.

words.meaning: the music of a song, the notes you can sing or hum
words.example: I don’t know the words, but I know the **tune**.

words.meaning: to know someone or something because you saw or heard it before
words.example: I didn’t **recognize** you with short hair!

words.meaning: the money you pay for a ride in a taxi, bus, train or plane
words.example: The bus **fare** is two dollars.

words.meaning: the way a person says words, which often shows where they come from
words.short: a way of speaking from a place
words.example: He speaks English with a Spanish **accent**.

words.meaning: a person who works in a library and helps people find books and information
words.short: a person who works in a library
words.example: The **librarian** helped me find a book about cooking.

words.meaning: a bill you get every month for electricity, gas or water at your home
words.short: a bill for electricity, gas or water
words.example: I paid the **utility bill** for the electricity.

words.meaning: to take a book or other thing from a library for a short time, after the library writes it down
words.example: You can **check out** ten books at a time.

words.meaning: a flat board on a wall or in a cabinet where you put books or other things
words.short: a board for books or things
words.example: The cookbooks are on the top **shelf**.

words.meaning: a meal where every person or family brings one dish of food to share
words.short: a meal where everyone brings food
words.example: Our class had a **potluck**, and I brought rice.

translations.es: comida en la que cada uno lleva un plato

words.meaning: nervous or quiet around other people, especially people you don’t know
words.example: My son is **shy**, so he doesn’t talk much at school.

words.meaning: food that is made in a special way, as part of a meal
words.example: Rice with beans is my favorite **dish**.

words.meaning: a list of the foods you need and the steps to cook something
words.example: This soup is my grandmother’s **recipe**.

words.meaning: something nice you say about a person or about what they did
words.example: My boss gave me a **compliment** on my work.

words.meaning: covered with rust, the brown layer that grows on old metal when it gets wet
words.example: The old gate was **rusty** and hard to open.

words.meaning: a metal tool you use to hold and turn nuts and bolts
words.example: He used a **wrench** to fix the pipe under the sink.

words.meaning: the part of a bicycle that you hold with your hands to steer it
words.short: the part of a bike you hold
words.example: Hold the **handlebars** with both hands.

words.meaning: to stop working at your job for good, usually when you are older
words.example: My father wants to **retire** when he is sixty-five.

words.meaning: a person who gets care from a doctor or nurse, often in a hospital
words.short: a person a doctor or nurse cares for
words.example: The nurse brought water to the **patient**.

words.meaning: the act of saying goodbye, often at a special party when someone leaves
words.example: We had a **farewell** lunch for our teacher.

words.meaning: the work a person does for many years of their life
words.example: She had a long **career** as a teacher.

words.meaning: something or someone that makes you feel calmer when you are sad or scared
words.short: something that helps you feel calm
words.example: Her phone calls were a **comfort** to me when I was sick.

words.meaning: To press the numbers on a phone to call someone.
words.example: She **dialed** her mother’s number.

words.meaning: To say you are sorry for something you did.
words.example: He **apologized** for being late.

words.meaning: To end a phone call.
words.example: Please don’t **hang up**. I have one more question.

words.meaning: The sound a person makes when they talk or sing.
words.short: the sound of a person talking
words.example: My teacher has a very calm **voice**.

words.meaning: A person who lives next to you or near you.
words.short: a person who lives near you
words.example: Our **neighbor** waters our plants when we travel.

words.meaning: A long strap or rope that you hold when you walk a dog.
words.short: a strap for walking a dog
words.example: Keep your dog on a **leash** in the park.

words.meaning: A band that goes around a dog’s or cat’s neck.
words.short: a band around a pet’s neck
words.example: The cat’s **collar** has its name on it.

words.meaning: The act of looking carefully for someone or something.
words.example: The **search** for the lost keys took an hour.

words.meaning: To hit a door with your hand so the people inside hear you.
words.short: hit a door to be heard
words.example: Please **knock** before you come in.

words.meaning: Knowledge and skill you get from doing a job or activity for a long time.
words.example: She has five years of **experience** as a cook.

words.meaning: Something you are very good at; a good quality you have.
words.example: Her biggest **strength** is that she is very patient.

words.meaning: To give someone a job.
words.example: The restaurant **hired** two new waiters.

words.meaning: Not able to move or get out of a place.
words.example: Our car was **stuck** in the mud.

words.meaning: A machine that makes a room, car, or bus warm.
words.example: Turn on the **heater**. It’s cold in here.

words.meaning: A big truck that pushes snow off the road.
words.example: The **snowplow** cleared our street early in the morning.

words.meaning: To give part of what you have to someone else, or to use something together.
words.example: The two sisters **shared** a pizza.
